title: Daily News (Los Angeles), Mar. 22, 1932 — Mayor Porter vetoes the Pasadena avenue renaming; the Downtown Business Men's association protests

excerpts.text: Mayor John C. Porter yesterday announced his veto of an ordinance changing the name of Pasadena avenue, between Avenue 39 and York boulevard, and of Annandale boulevard, from York junction to Colorado boulevard, to "North Figueroa street." The ordinance recently was passed by city council, despite protests of numerous property owners, as well as historical and civic groups.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Business Men Back Porter in Decision." Two QUALIFIED changes to one name.

excerpts.text: The elimination of old landmarks or historical names in a city with a background of color and romance, such as we have here in Los Angeles, is not for the best interests of the people. History has been enriched through the preservation of street names which carry a distinctive significance, and should be encouraged.
excerpts.note: ★★ Mayor Porter's veto message, quoted by the paper. The historic-preservation case for street names, 1932.

excerpts.text: We have streets leading from Los Angeles carrying such names as Wilmington boulevard, Santa Monica boulevard, Long Beach boulevard, Redondo boulevard and Venice boulevard—all indicating the destination of the highway.
excerpts.note: ★ THE DESTINATION PRINCIPLE, with five examples named by the mayor.

excerpts.text: Pasadena avenue has been so designated for many years, and, in my opinion, the name should not be disturbed. Furthermore, our cordial relations with the city of Pasadena should receive careful consideration. . . .
excerpts.note: Continuation of the veto message.

excerpts.text: Declaring that the change is opposed by the property owners affected and will work a hardship upon the downtown area, the Downtown Business Men's association yesterday transmitted to council a resolution also opposing the ordinance.

Whereas, out of a total of 34,000 feet on Pasadena avenue from the river to the city limits, a total of 20,400 feet of frontage has already signed as opposing the change, and Whereas, the citizens of Pasadena have declared their city will be most adversely affected by the change.
excerpts.note: ★ 20,400 of 34,000 feet of frontage opposed — 60% — and the change passed anyway.

excerpts.text: Now, therefore, be it resolved by the executive committee of the board of directors of the Downtown Business Men's association of Los Angeles that it protest against the passage of the ordinance and does hereby urge the honorable city council to reconsider and rescind its action in passing the said ordinance in order that the status quo be maintained, namely that the name of Pasadena avenue remain as it is.

title: Daily News (Los Angeles), Mar. 23, 1932 — "Council Overrides Street Change Veto": Pasadena avenue and Annandale boulevard become North Figueroa street, 11 to 4

excerpts.text: Despite Mayor John C. Porter's veto, the city council yesterday adopted an ordinance changing the name of Pasadena avenue between Avenue 39 and York boulevard and of Annandale boulevard from York Junction to Colorado boulevard to "North Figueroa street."
excerpts.note: ★★ Headline: "Council Overrides Street Change Veto." "Yesterday" = Mar. 22, 1932.

excerpts.text: The mayor maintained that the name "Pasadena avenue" was of historical importance, in addition to the fact that it has long designated a thoroughfare which leads to the city of Pasadena.

The vote to override the mayor's veto in the council was preceded by a three-cornered battle in which Councilman Edward L. Thrasher, who favored the change, opposed Councilmen Carl I. Jacobson and George W. C. Baker. The final vote in favor of the ordinance was 11 to 4.

title: J. M. Guinn, “The Plan of Old Los Angeles: And the Story of Its Highways and Byways,” Annual Publication of the Historical Society of Southern California, Vol. 3, No. 3 (1895), pp. 40–50

excerpts.text: The names of the streets on Ord's plan are given in both Spanish and English; beginning with Main they are as follows: Calle Principal — Main street; Calle Primavera — Spring street, named for the season spring; Calle Fortin — Fort street; Calle Loma — Hill street; Calle Aceytuna — Olive street; Calle de Las Caridad — The Street of Charity (now Grand avenue); Calle de Las Esperanzas — The Street of Hopes; Calle de Los Flores — The Street of Flowers; Calle de Los Chapules — The Street of Grasshoppers (now Pearl street). North of the plaza church the north and south streets were the Calle de Eternidad — Eternity street, so named because it had neither beginning nor end, or, rather, each end terminated in the hills. Calle del Toro — Bull street, significant of the national pastime of Spain and Mexico — the bull fight. Calle de Las Arispas — Hornet street; an exceedingly lively street at times when the hornets had business engagements with the paisanos. Calle de Las Adobes — Adobe street, well named. The east and west streets were Calle Corta — Short street; Calle Alta — High street; Calle de Las Virgines — Street of Virgins; Calle del Colegio — College street, the only street that retains its primitive name.
excerpts.note: ★★★ SEVENTEEN NAMES IN TWO LANGUAGES, and four etymologies stated outright: Spring for the season, Eternity for having no end, Bull for the bull fight, Hornet for the hornets. ★ COLLEGE STREET IS FLAGGED BY GUINN HIMSELF as “the only street that retains its primitive name” — a claim about the whole grid, made in 1895, and a strong one to test against this corpus. ⚠ THREE SUCCESSORS ARE GIVEN: Charity → Grand Avenue, Grasshoppers → Pearl Street, and (below) Orchards → San Pedro. ⚠ OCR: the PDF prints “Того” for Toro, “Accytuna” for Aceytuna and “Colégio” for Colegio; corrected here against the sense and recorded so nobody reads the corrections as a variant spelling.

excerpts.text: Note. — For information in regard to the old names of streets I am indebted to C. C. Grove of the West Coast Abstract company.
excerpts.note: ★ THE SOURCE BEHIND THE SOURCE, and the reason to cite the excerpt rather than “Guinn says”: the street-name concordance is a title abstractor's work relayed by a historian. Good provenance for the pairings, weaker for the stories attached to them.

excerpts.text: The Calle de Las Chapules was for many years the extreme western street of the city. The name originated thus: On certain years, mostly during the dry or drouth years, myriads of grasshoppers hatched on the low grassy plains of the Ballona and Cienegas. When they had devoured all vegetation where they originated, they took flight, and, flying with the wind, moved in great clouds towards the east — like the locusts of Egypt, devouring everything in their course. When the destroying hosts reached the Calle de Las Chapules, the vinatero knew his grape crop for that season was doomed.
excerpts.note: An etymology with a mechanism, which is what makes it checkable rather than decorative: the street was the city's western edge, so it was where the swarms arriving from the Ballona were first met.

excerpts.text: Calle Primavera — Spring street, sixty or seventy years ago was known as the Calle de Las Caridad — the Street of Charity. The aristocratic part of the city in those days was in the neighborhood of the plaza, and on Upper Main street. Spring street being well out in the suburbs, its inhabitants were mostly peons and Mexicans of the poorer class, who were dependent largely upon the charity of their wealthier neighbors. There is a tradition, which I have not been able to verify by written record, that back about the beginning of the century, Spring street was known as Calle Cuidado — Lookout or Beware street.
excerpts.note: ✔ RESOLVED — TWO STREETS, NOT A CONTRADICTION, and Guinn's own 1912 paper decides it (Kenny, 2026-09-17). Read against the concordance above, this looks like the same Spanish name on two streets; it is. documents/guinn-1912 says outright that “North Spring street, in the early years of the last century Calle Caridad (Charity street)” is one of “the oldest streets of the city” — so the pre-1849 Caridad is the NORTH SPRING line, through what is now Chinatown, while the concordance's Caridad is the Ord Survey's own christening two blocks west of Olive, which became Grand Avenue. ★★ AND GUINN SETTLES IT AGAINST HIMSELF WITHOUT ANY OUTSIDE HELP: the 1912 paper also states that “all the streets south of First street to Twelfth street and all west of Main street to Figueroa date their existence from the Ord Survey, made in 1849.” Downtown Spring Street did not exist before 1849, so it cannot have carried a name “sixty or seventy years” before 1895. The only part of the Spring line old enough is the stretch north of First. ⚠ SO THE LOOSE WORD IS THIS PAPER'S: Guinn writes “Spring street” here where the 1912 paper writes “North Spring street”, and the later, narrower statement is the one to follow. ✔ ORD'S OWN SHEET AGREES: the county recorder's copy, M.R. 53-68, labels this street “Calle Primavera” and carries “Charity St / Calle de Caridad” as a SEPARATE street on the same sheet (cited in streets-data.js). ★ Note also that Guinn marks his own hedge on Calle Cuidado — “which I have not been able to verify by written record” — which is how to read everything in this paper that he does not so mark; the Caridad claim is NOT so marked.

excerpts.text: With the growth of the town southward, the business center drifted from its first locality on Upper Main street, and for a time became fixed at the head of Los Angeles street where that street intersected with Aliso, Arcadia, Sanchez and Negro alley. At that point Los Angeles was then a very broad street probably two hundred feet wide; it narrowed as it ran southward and widened again at its intersection with First street. In the early part of the century it was known as Zanja (ditch) street. In the early thirties it had been dignified into the Calle Principal or Main street and with its continuation the Calle de Los Huertos — the street of orchards — (now San Pedro) formed the principal highway running southward from the center of the town.
excerpts.note: ★ A THIRD NAME FOR LOS ANGELES STREET, earlier than any in documents/guinn-1912's account: ZANJA STREET, for the ditch, before it was “dignified into” Calle Principal. ⚠ And note what that does to the concordance: Calle Principal is given above as MAIN street, and here it is what LOS ANGELES street was called in the 1830s. The name moved between two roadways, which is exactly the kind of thing that makes a name entity a lineage rather than a string. ★ SAN PEDRO STREET was Calle de Los Huertos, the street of orchards. ⚠ OCR prints “Zanjo”; the word is zanja.

excerpts.text: There was one street in the older portion of Los Angeles that is not named in Ord's plan, but which, in the flush days of gold mining from 1850 to '55, had a more wide-spread notoriety than any other street in the city. It was the Calle de Los Negros in Spanish… It was a short and narrow street extending from the then termination of Los Angeles street to the plaza. In length it did not exceed 500 feet… With the decadence of gold mining the character of the street changed… It ceased to be the rendezvous of the gambler and the desperado and became the center of the Chinese quarter of the city.
excerpts.note: Quoted in part. The street's Americanised name is a racial slur that was in general printed use in 1895 and is elided here with an ellipsis; the Spanish name is the one to use. This is the street of the 1871 Chinese Massacre, which Guinn goes on to describe. ⚠ It is NOT on Ord's plan, which Guinn states — so it is an organic name, not a surveyed one, and any entity for it should say so.

excerpts.text: In the city clerk's office is a copy of a map of the first subdivision of Los Angeles city lands made after the American occupation. It is entitled, “Plan de la Ciudad de Los Angeles, by E. O. C. Ord, Lt. U. S. A., Wm. R. Hutton, Asst., August 29, 1849.” Ord's survey embraces all that portion of the city bounded north by First street and the base of the first line of hills, east by Main street, south by Twelfth street and west by Pearl street. Also that portion of the city north of Short street and west of Upper Main to the base of the hills… The blocks, except the first tier, are 600 feet in length, and are divided into ten lots each, 120 feet front by 165 feet in depth.
excerpts.note: ★ THE EXTENT OF ORD'S SURVEY, stated as four bounds — First, Main, Twelfth, Pearl — which is a usable test for whether a given street was inside the original American survey or added later. Several documents in this corpus describe themselves as extensions of Ord's Survey (documents/mr003-240 is “Block 35½, Being an Extension of Ord's Survey”), and this fixes what they were extending.

excerpts.text: On a map of the pueblo of Los Angeles, made in 1786, when Arguello surveyed the lands of the founders, there is a road marked as beginning at the southeast corner of the old plaza, from thence running southeasterly until it intersects what is now Aliso street; thence following the present line of that street it crosses the river and passes out of the pueblo to the southeast… This, in the days of King Carlos III, was the Camino del Rey, or Camino real.
excerpts.note: ★ ALISO STREET IS OLDER THAN ANY PLAT, and older than the pueblo's own survey: it is the line of the royal road out to San Juan Capistrano and San Diego, marked on a map of 1786. Bears on the whole Frenchtown cluster east of Alameda, which was laid out against this line.

title: J. M. Guinn, “The Passing of Our Historic Street Names,” Annual Publication of the Historical Society of Southern California, Vol. 9, No. 1/2 (1912–1913), pp. 59–64

excerpts.text: Calle Libertad became Requena street in honor of Manuel Requena, a municipal statesman of the old regime, who filled the offices of Alcalde and Regidor under Mexican rule and Councilman under American. He was a large landowner on the line of the street and a most estimable gentleman.
excerpts.note: ★ STATES OUTRIGHT what `requena-street` had recorded as an inference from the ownership.

excerpts.text: The meaningless name of East Market street was recently conferred upon it to connect it with West Market — a little tag of a street extending from Main to Spring street — another exemplification of the caudle appendage wagging the canine.
excerpts.note: ★ THE MOTIVE FOR “MARKET”, and it is not a market: the name was taken from an existing West Market Street so the two would match. Guinn, who disliked it, calls it meaningless.

excerpts.text: East Market street of today was originally Calle Libertad (Liberty street).
excerpts.note: With the two excerpts above this gives the full sequence: Libertad → Requena → East Market.

excerpts.text: Our modern municipal statesmen seem to harbor hatred to Spanish street names — recently nearly all of Buena Vista street fell before the advance of North Broadway; Requena street gave up to East Market street and what was once Corta street and a portion of Alta street were absorbed into Sunset Boulevard.

All the streets south of First street to Twelfth street and all west of Main street to Figueroa, date their existence from the Ord Survey, made in 1849. They were christened both in English and Spanish. The Spanish names long since ceased to be used and are forgotten. Forten, Caridad and Chapules have been changed to Broadway, Grand avenue and Figueroa.
excerpts.note: ★ A DATING RULE FOR THE WHOLE DOWNTOWN GRID, and the most useful single sentence in either Guinn paper for this corpus: nothing south of First or west of Main existed before 1849. Any claim that a street in that rectangle carried a name earlier than the Ord Survey is wrong about the street. That is what resolves the Caridad tangle — see `oldest-streets` below. ⚠ “Forten” is Fortin (Calle Fortin, Fort Street); the OCR and possibly the printer mangled it. documents/guinn-1895 gives the full concordance of which this is a three-item summary.

excerpts.text: long before the Gringo came, Los Angeles street was known as Calle Zanja (Ditch street), next as Calle de Las Vinas (Street of Vineyards), later as Calle de Las Huertas (Street of Orchards), and before the Ord Survey as the Calle Principal (Main street). It was the principal street leading south to the embarcadero of San Pedro.
excerpts.note: Four pre-Ord names for `los-angeles-street`, none of which has an entity.

excerpts.text: San Fernando street (formerly Upper Main), North Main (once Alegro or Junction street) and North Spring street, in the early years of the last century Calle Caridad (Charity street), are the oldest streets of the city.
excerpts.note: ★★ THE SENTENCE THAT SEPARATES THE TWO CARIDADS, and the reason `charity` and any Caridad on the Spring line are two entities rather than one. Guinn names three streets as the city's oldest, all north of the plaza, and gives NORTH SPRING the name Calle Caridad in the early 1800s — while the Caridad of `ord-survey-names` above, the one that became Grand Avenue, is the Ord Survey's own 1849 christening two blocks west of Olive. ★ IT ALSO RESOLVES documents/guinn-1895, where the same author writes loosely that “Spring street, sixty or seventy years ago was known as the Calle de Las Caridad”: the passage above dates everything south of First to the Ord Survey, so downtown Spring did not exist to be named in the 1830s and the north end is the only candidate. (Kenny read it this way on 2026-09-17, before the 1912 text was checked; the paper says it in so many words.) ⭐ TWO MORE LINEAGES IN ONE SENTENCE, neither yet an entity: SAN FERNANDO STREET was formerly UPPER MAIN, and NORTH MAIN was once ALEGRO or JUNCTION STREET — the “Calle de Las Allegria — Junction street” of the 1895 paper.

excerpts.text: That portion of Marchessault street which was recently absorbed by Sunset Boulevard early in its history bore the name of Calle Iglesias, or Church street, so named from its proximity to the Church of Our Lady of the Angels; then it became Pan, or Bread street; next it expanded into Panaderia (Bakery) street. When Ord made his “piano” of the city it was known as Corta (Short) street — it was only a block long.
excerpts.note: ⚠ This Corta is by the Plaza and is NOT `corto-street`, which is between Beaudry and Boylston a mile west.

excerpts.text: The street on the north side of the plaza, upon which some of the residences of the pueblo aristocracy fronted, was known as Calle Trinidad (Trinity) street, and was one of a trio of streets that united to form Main street. Its name was changed to honor the memory of Marchessault, who, like Whittington of feline fame, was three times Mayor, not of “London town,” but of Los Angeles. He cut his official term and his span of life short by suicide.

The Calle Eternidad (Eternity street) extended from the foot of the hill where the Calle Alta intersected it to the Campo Santo, or Calvary Cemetery. The name was fitting. For half a century the dead of the pueblo were carried over it to their eternal rest. The name was changed to Buena Vista street and it was extended to the river.
excerpts.note: Bears on `eternity` and `high-street-chinatown` (Calle Alta).

excerpts.text: Temple street fifty years ago, when it ended at the First Protestant Church, which stood on the corner of New High street where the stone lions now guard the steps up to the court house, was known as Salvation street. It was a time of “spiritual darkness” in the city and the name was probably given in derision.
excerpts.note: A predecessor of `temple` with no entity.

excerpts.text: The jail at that time was on the block bounded by North Spring, New High and Franklin streets, the latter street then known as Jail street.
Away back in the early years of American occupation, Soda Water street intersected Lemon street near the end of Moran's lane, now East Ninth street.
excerpts.note: ★ Bears on `lemon-st-arts-district` and `moran-s-lane`: it puts Lemon Street on the ground decades before the 1887 sheets that letter it, and dates Moran's Lane's end.

excerpts.text: Deepwater street was a short, narrow street on a sloping hillside. How it got into deep water I do not know. Some joker, probably, christened it by the rule of contraries.

Lovers' Lane was a shady street that in early times meandered northward toward the river from what are now the suburbs of Chinatown. The lumber yards, the machine shops and the “Heathen Chinee” encroached upon it and the lovers ceased their trysts in it. Its name was changed to Date street, but the dates have long since gone to join the lovers.

The use of the two languages in our street nomenclature has resulted in duplication of names. We have Estrella street in Spanish, and a few blocks away Star street in English; Towne avenue in one part of the city and Pueblo in another. Annexation of outside territory has increased our duplicates. We have at the present time no less than three Mountain Views in English and two Monte Vistas in Spanish.
excerpts.note: The duplicate problem that drove the 1888 cull and the 1897 commission, stated by a man who served on one of them.

excerpts.text: A few years ago I was appointed by a Mayor of our city a member of a street-naming commission… A street in the southwestern part of the city bore a compound name, “Georgia Bell.” The commission changed it to a single name and thereby incurred the wrath of Georgia's husband. He employed an attorney to undo our work and to demolish the commission itself.
excerpts.note: ★ THE GEORGIA BELL REVERSION FROM THE INSIDE. `georgia-bell` records the 1897 reversion to “Georgia”; this is a commissioner saying his commission did it and that Horace Bell fought it. ⚠ Guinn is a participant here, not a neutral witness.

excerpts.text: The members of that commission labored industriously to bring order out of the chaos of street names caused by the ambition of real estate promoters to immortalize themselves, their sisters, their cousins and their aunts in our street nomenclature. To give local coloring and some historic significance to our city highways we injected into the mass of names imported from eastern cities and towns a few smooth-syllabled native Californian names of Spanish origin, but the dwellers on the streets whose names were changed would have none of that.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, May 2, 1923 — ordinance adopted changing Bluff street between Grand View and Coronado to Fourth street

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the name of Bluff street between Grand View street and Coronado street to Fourth street was adopted by the City Council yesterday. An ordinance was adopted placing in Zone 3 the property bounded by Grand avenue, Main street, Washington street and Jefferson street.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Bluff Street Renamed Fourth by Ordinance." "Yesterday" = May 1, 1923. Zone numeral read as 3; the digit is faint.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, Apr. 4, 1924 — Mayor Cryer expected to sign the ordinance changing Orange street to Wilshire boulevard

excerpts.text: Mayor Cryer is considering the proposed change of the name of Orange street to Wilshire boulevard. He indicated yesterday that he would sign the ordinance changing the street name.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Cryer Expected to O K Orange St. Name Change."

title: Los Angeles Examiner, Apr. 7, 1924 — Mayor Cryer defers signing the Orange street ordinance while he looks into a viaduct across Westlake Park

excerpts.text: Pending consideration, Mayor George E. Cryer has held up the ordinance changing the name of Orange street, between Alvarado and Figueroa streets, to Wilshire boulevard.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Mayor Defers Signing Name Change Ordinance." QUALIFIED: Alvarado to Figueroa.

excerpts.text: He is looking into the possibility of a viaduct being constructed across Westlake Park to connect Orange street with Wilshire boulevard. The Mayor indicated that he will sign the change in name ordinance this week.
excerpts.note: ★ The name change and the physical connection considered together. Westlake Park is today's MacArthur Park.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, Apr. 12, 1924 — Mayor Cryer signs the ordinance changing Orange street between Alvarado and Figueroa to Wilshire boulevard

excerpts.text: Mayor George E. Cryer late yesterday signed the ordinance changing the name of Orange street between Alvarado and Figueroa streets to Wilshire boulevard. This ordinance was adopted by the council ten days ago.
excerpts.note: ★★ Headline: "Orange Street Name Changed." Signed Apr. 11, 1924; adopted about Apr. 1, 1924.

excerpts.text: In this connection the council has under consideration the matter of starting proceedings for the widening of Orange street and connecting it up with Wilshire boulevard west of Park View avenue by means of a viaduct across Westlake Park.
excerpts.note: Park View avenue named as the point of connection.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, June 8, 1926 — "'Waverly Drive' Asked": ordinance under consideration for Waverly avenue between Farwell and Rowena

excerpts.text: City Council has under consideration an ordinance changing the name of Waverly avenue between Farwell avenue and Rowena avenue to "Waverly Drive."
excerpts.note: Headline: "'Waverly Drive' Asked." A suffix change, not a renaming.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, July 23, 1926 — council unanimously adopts the ordinance changing South Park avenue and Canal street to Avalon boulevard

excerpts.text: By a unanimous vote the City Council yesterday adopted the ordinance changing the name of South Park avenue and the name of Canal street to "Avalon boulevard."
excerpts.note: ★ Headline: "Council O. K.'s Ordinance Changing Street Name." Unanimous. "Yesterday" = July 22, 1926.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, June 22, 1927 — public hearing set on the ordinance changing Main street to Huntington boulevard

excerpts.text: A public hearing on the proposed ordinance changing the name of Main street to Huntington boulevard will be held by the City Council next Tuesday morning. In the meantime the proposed ordinance will be drafted by the city attorney.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Main Street Name Change Hearing Set." "Next Tuesday" = June 28, 1927.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, June 29, 1927 — "Main Street Vote Today": council orders the Huntington boulevard ordinance drafted, 10 to 4, after a spirited hearing

excerpts.text: At the conclusion of a spirited public hearing, the City Council yesterday by a vote of 10 to 4 ordered the drafting of an ordinance changing the name of Main street to "Huntington boulevard." The ordinance will be presented to the council today.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Main Street Vote Today." "Yesterday" = June 28, 1927.

excerpts.text: The four councilmen opposing the change were Ash, Colden, Randall and President Workman.

Among those opposing the change in name were Herman C. Lichtenberger, who said the Native Sons of the Golden West and the Native Daughters were opposed to the change; O. E. Johnson, I. B. Benjamin, V. Bell and Joseph Mesmer.
excerpts.note: ★ An organized heritage constituency appearing at a street-naming hearing, 1927.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, Oct. 18, 1927 — "1500 Fight New Main St. Name": a petition headed by J. A. Graves, with the engineering department, a federal judge and the bishop against the change

excerpts.text: A petition urging the City Council not to change the name of Main street was filed with the City Council yesterday. The petition is signed by about 1500 persons and is headed by President J. A. Graves of the Farmers & Merchants National Bank.
excerpts.note: Headline: "1500 Fight New Main St. Name." "Yesterday" = Oct. 17, 1927.

excerpts.text: Mr. Graves pointed out that the petition is not signed by people at so much a head, but actual property owners on Main street or people doing business thereon.
excerpts.note: An 1920s distinction between a paid signature drive and a property owners' petition.

excerpts.text: The drafting of an ordinance changing the name of Main street to Huntington boulevard was ordered by the former council, but the measure was withheld.
excerpts.note: ★★ ORDERED, DRAFTED, WITHHELD. The 1927 change never became law.

excerpts.text: Because Main street is so-named in a number of descriptions of property affected by improvements now under way or proposed for the near future, the city engineering department has requested that no change be made in the name for the present.
excerpts.note: ★ Street-improvement law defeats a renaming — third instance in this corpus.

excerpts.text: Judge William P. James, of the United States District Court, also asked that no change be made in the name. In his letter he declared: "Main street is associated in both a sentimental and commercial way with the city's life from its earliest day."
excerpts.note: The word before "earliest" is damaged in the scan; "its" from context.

excerpts.text: The tendency of the present day to change street names as a means of paying tribute to the memory of some distinguished citizens tends to mar the historic connection between the old and the new.
excerpts.note: ★ The Right Rev. John J. Cantwell, bishop of Los Angeles and San Diego, quoted in part by the paper.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, Aug. 6, 1928 — city planning committee recommends changing Adams street to Adams Boulevard

excerpts.text: Recommendation of the city planning committee that the City Council adopt the proposed ordinance changing the name of Adams street to "Adams Boulevard" will be considered by the council today.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Adams Street Renaming."

title: Los Angeles Examiner, Aug. 18, 1928 — "Sunset Blvd. Name Change Ordered": council votes 8 to 5 to draft an ordinance making Sunset boulevard between the Plaza and Hillhurst into Hollywood Boulevard

excerpts.text: At the conclusion of a public hearing the City Council yesterday by a vote of eight to five directed the city engineer and city attorney to draft an ordinance changing the name of Sunset boulevard between the Plaza and Hillhurst avenue to "Hollywood Boulevard." Councilmen Hall and Davis were absent.
excerpts.note: ★★ Headline: "Sunset Blvd. Name Change Ordered." QUALIFIED: the Plaza to Hillhurst avenue. "Yesterday" = Aug. 17, 1928.

excerpts.text: The council rejected by an eight to five vote a majority report from the city planning committee recommending that a petition from a majority of the property owners along the entire length of Sunset boulevard be obtained before any action was taken. The committee also suggested that the sentiment of property owners along Hollywood boulevard be obtained.
excerpts.note: The consultation step was deliberately skipped.

excerpts.text: On motion of Councilman Randall seconded by Councilman Foster the council then directed the ordinance drafted.

Those favoring the change in name were Henry E. Holbrook, Greely Kolts, former councilman, A. J. Barnes and Captain E. Z. Collings. Petitions signed by a number of improvement associations favoring the change in name were also presented to the council.

Among those opposing the change were Carl Bush of the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce; Harry Bain of the Hollywood Boulevard Improvement Association; E. F. Bogardus, Miss Helen Hogan, A. Z. Taft and C. E. Toberman.
excerpts.note: ★ Hollywood's own chamber of commerce and boulevard association opposed extending the Hollywood Boulevard name downtown.

excerpts.text: Former Councilman Barnes maintained that the change in name "will be an asset to Hollywood." Councilman Shaw also declared that Hollywood would benefit by the proposed change in name of the boulevard. Randall claimed that the arguments against the change in name "are based on materialism."
excerpts.note: Councilman Shaw is presumably the former city engineer Shaw of documents/dnla-1926-05-06 — unverified.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, Aug. 21, 1929 — Tenth Street Improvement Association petitions to change Country Club drive between Lucerne and Robertson to Olympic boulevard

excerpts.text: Petition from the Tenth Street Improvement Association for an ordinance changing the name of Country Club drive, between Lucerne avenue and Robertson boulevard to "Olympic boulevard," was referred yesterday by City Council to the city engineer and planning commission.
excerpts.note: ★ Headline: "Would Re-Name Street." "Yesterday" = Aug. 20, 1929.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, Oct. 21, 1929 — "'Esmeralda' Reverts to 'East Rose Hill'": a 100 per cent petition to restore the former name

excerpts.text: The city planning committee has recommended that the city engineer be directed to prepare an ordinance changing the name of Esmeralda street back to East Rose Hill drive between Raynol street and Topaz street. A 100 per cent petition favored restoring the former name.
excerpts.note: ★★ "back to" — a RESTORATION. 100 per cent petition. QUALIFIED: Raynol to Topaz.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, May 3, 1930 — "Gage Avenue Now": five streets adopted into one name to make a through highway across the city

excerpts.text: Ordinance changing the names of Merrill avenue, Sixty-third street, Sixty-third place, Sixty-fourth street, and Hyde Park boulevard to "Gage avenue," was adopted by the City Council, yesterday. With slight jogs the various thoroughfares involved make one through highway across the city.
excerpts.note: ★ Headline: "Gage Avenue Now." Five streets, one name. "Yesterday" = May 2, 1930. "make one" is a best reading — one word is faint.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, June 11, 1930 — "'Crenshaw Blvd.' Name Extended": Angeles Mesa drive from Adams street to the south city limits becomes Crenshaw boulevard, with Inglewood asked to continue it

excerpts.text: City Council yesterday adopted an ordinance changing the name of Angeles Mesa drive between Adams street and south city limits at Seventy-ninth street to "Crenshaw boulevard." The city of Inglewood will be asked to continue the change in the name between Seventy-ninth street and Eighty-first street.
excerpts.note: ★ Headline: "'Crenshaw Blvd.' Name Extended." "Yesterday" = June 10, 1930. Inglewood asked to follow.

title: Los Angeles Examiner, Nov. 13, 1930 — council declares for changing Hollenbeck avenue for its entire length to Eighth street, on a 57.4 per cent petition

excerpts.text: In response to a 57.4 property owners' petition, City Council yesterday declared in favor of changing the name of Hollenbeck avenue for its entire length to Eighth street. City Engineer J. J. Jessup was directed to present the necessary ordinance changing the name.
excerpts.note: ★ Headline: "Hollenbeck Avenue Will Be Eighth St." "For its entire length" — an explicit whole-name scope. "Yesterday" = Nov. 12, 1930.

title: Los Angeles Evening Express, Apr. 1, 1924 — front page: council unanimously passes the ordinance changing Orange street between Alvarado and Figueroa to Wilshire boulevard, "city-sea road"

excerpts.text: By unanimous vote the city council today passed an ordinance changing the name of Orange street between Alvarado and Figueroa streets to Wilshire boulevard.
excerpts.note: ★★ Headline: "Orange Street Is Changed to Wilshire Blvd. / Improvement Program Given Impetus / City-Sea Road, Plan." UNANIMOUS, Apr. 1, 1924.

excerpts.text: By changing the name of Orange street, it was stated by city officials the city had practically established a continuous thoroughfare from the heart of the business district of the city to the ocean.
excerpts.note: ★ The 1924 argument: continuity to the sea. Contrast the 1908 objection in documents/lah-1908-07-14.

excerpts.text: The action today, it was declared, opens the way for the completion of Wilshire boulevard, which, it was predicted, would be the most magnificent thoroughfare in the entire west.

title: Los Angeles Evening Express, Sept. 15, 1925 — "Fight to Keep Street Names City Changed": Sawtelle residents petition to repeal the Old Soldiers' Home district renaming

excerpts.text: Asserting that the City Council changed the names of all the streets in the Old Soldiers' Home district without warning, residents of Sawtelle today petitioned the Council to repeal the ordinance changing the names and to give the residents of the district an opportunity to select the designations they prefer.
excerpts.note: ★ Headline: "Fight to Keep Street Names City Changed." The sequel to documents/lah-1919-09-30.

excerpts.text: The petition asserts that Council passed the ordinance changing the street names under emergency provisions and that the new names became effective the day aftr the ordinances were adopted.
excerpts.note: ★★ EMERGENCY PROVISIONS — effective the next day, no waiting period. "aftr" as printed. Note "ordinances", plural.

excerpts.text: According to the petition, the change in street names has caused utmost confusion. Residents of the district say they "don't know whether we live in California or Halifax."
excerpts.note: The residents' own words, as the paper reports them.

excerpts.text: The petitions were referred to the city planning commission.

title: Los Angeles Evening Express, Oct. 16, 1925 — ordinance adopted changing Childs avenue to Griffith Park boulevard; Griffin avenue expected to follow as Montecito drive

excerpts.text: City Council has adopted an ordinance changing the name of Childs avenue to Griffith Park boulevard. As a result of this change it is probable Griffin avenue will be changed to Montecito drive to prevent confusion with Griffith Park boulevard.
excerpts.note: ★ Headline: "Change Name of Avenue." A cascade, with the second step only "probable" — and Griffin Avenue survives today, so it did not follow.

title: Los Angeles Herald, “Common Council,” Feb. 14, 1874 (petition to rename Grasshopper, Bull and Wasp streets)

excerpts.text: A petition was received from a number of property owners, requesting that Grasshopper street be changed to Union Avenue, Bull street to Castelar, and Wasp street to Yale street. The petition was favorably received and a special committee, in conjunction with the City Attorney, was appointed to draft an ordinance to comply with the request.

title: Los Angeles Herald, “City and Suburbs,” Feb. 27, 1874 (council renames Grasshopper St → Pearl St)

excerpts.text: The owners of property on Grasshopper street petition for the name Pearl street; others for Union Avenue. A heavy discussion ensued when the first named petitioners won, and Pearl street is to be the new name.
An ordinance changing Grasshopper street to Pearl street was carried.

rows.note: Two acts in one meeting: the petitioners' name is settled in the first passage, and the second carries the ordinance that makes it so. The document's date is the council day (Feb. 26), not the paper's (Feb. 27).

title: Los Angeles Herald, May 13, 1883, p. 3 — the Council passes an ordinance changing Turner Street, from First to Alameda, to Jackson Street

excerpts.text: The Council last night passed an ordinance changing the name of Turner street, from First to Alameda, to Jackson street.
excerpts.note: Qualified, enacted, and dated to the evening of May 12, 1883. The ordinance's own number is not given and the minutes for the date have not been looked at.

title: Los Angeles Herald, June 17, 1883, p. 3 — the City Attorney instructed to draft an ordinance changing Polyxena Street to Clay Street

excerpts.text: Also, that the City Attorney be instructed to draft an ordinance changing the name of Polyxena-street to Clay-street. So ordered.
excerpts.note: The paper hyphenates both names, which is the compositor rather than the council. An instruction, not an act.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Aug. 19, 1883, p. 3 — the Board of Public Works recommends renaming Turner, Pacific, Pine, Georgia, Elm and Rose streets, and an ordinance changing Chavez Street to Main Street is referred to it

excerpts.text: The Board of Public Works report as follows: Recommend that the City Attorney be instructed to prepare an ordinance changing the names of the following streets:
Turner street, west of Main street, to Sonora street. Adopted.
excerpts.note: “Adopted” here means the Council adopted the Board's RECOMMENDATION, not an ordinance — the recommendation is that one be prepared.

excerpts.text: Pacific street, in Bell's addition, to Montgomery street. Adopted.
excerpts.note: Names the addition. The three items that follow say “in same addition”, so all four are in Bell's.

excerpts.text: Pine street, in same addition, to Cherry street. Adopted.
excerpts.note: A third Pine Street for this corpus, after the Miguel Subdivision's (16th Street's predecessor) and the one in the 1896 southwest ordinance. Three streets, one spelling, no connection between them.

excerpts.text: Georgia street, in same addition, to Alabama street. Adopted.
excerpts.note: ★ The proposal that did not survive: the ordinance as reported on Sept. 2 makes it Georgia Bell street instead (documents/lah-1883-09-02).

excerpts.text: Elm street, in same addition, to Bush street. Adopted.
Rose street, East Los Angeles, to Kuhrts street. Adopted.
excerpts.note: “East Los Angeles” in 1883 is modern Lincoln Heights. NOT this project's Rose Street, which is in the Arts District.

excerpts.text: In matter of Figueroa street ask one week's further time. Granted.
excerpts.note: Kept because of what it is not: the Board had something before it about Figueroa Street in Aug. 1883 and asked for another week. Fourteen years before Ord. 4093 moved the Figueroa name onto Pearl's ground. What the matter was is not stated here and is worth a look in the following weeks.

excerpts.text: Also, an ordinance changing the name of Chavez street to Main street. Referred to the Board of Public Works.
excerpts.note: A separate item from the Board's report — this one is going TO the Board. Main Street absorbing a named street rather than a new name being coined.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Aug. 26, 1883, p. 3 — an ordinance changing the names of Turner, Pacific, Elm, Pine, Georgia and Rose streets is adopted

excerpts.text: Ordinance changing the names of Turner, Pacific, Elm, Pine, Georgia and Rose streets. Adopted.
excerpts.note: Six streets named, none of the new names given. Compare the five-street list of Sept. 2, which gives the new names and drops Pacific.

excerpts.text: On motion, the City Attorney was instructed to commence the necessary action.
excerpts.note: The sentence immediately above, on a different matter; kept only so the clip is transcribed in full and nobody re-reads it wondering.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Sept. 2, 1883, p. 3 — ordinance adopted changing Turner to Sonora, Pine to Cherry, Georgia to Georgia Bell, Elm to Bush, and Rose (East Los Angeles) to Kuhrts

excerpts.text: Ordinance changing the names of certain streets: Turner street to Sonora street; Pine to Cherry street; Georgia to Georgia Bell street; Elm to Bush street; Rose street, East Los Angeles, to Kuhrts street. Adopted.
excerpts.note: ★ The instrument for Georgia → Georgia Bell, six years earlier than the date this project had been carrying. Five streets; the Aug. 26 report of the same or a related ordinance listed six, including Pacific.

excerpts.text: Recommend that the City Surveyor be instructed to mark the western boundary of the city.
excerpts.note: The line immediately above, transcribed so the clip is complete. Incidentally useful: the city's western boundary was still an unmarked line in 1883, which is the same boundary the 1896 southwest ordinances measure from as the “West Charter boundary”.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Oct. 21, 1883, p. 3 — the Council agrees to accept Morgan Lane as a public street and orders an ordinance changing its name to Mayo Street

excerpts.text: In matter of accepting Morgan Lane and changing name of same to Mayo street, recommend that the Council agree to comply with stipulation in document now on record, and that the City Attorney be instructed to draft an ordinance changing the name of Morgan Lane to Mayo street, the same to be widened to uniform width of sixty feet. So ordered.
excerpts.note: The Morgan Lane of documents/mr005-005, fourteen months after the Orchard Tract sheet drew it. Acceptance, widening and renaming in one motion.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Jan. 6, 1886, p. 5 — “An ordinance changing the name of certain streets. Adopted.”

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the name of certain streets. Adopted.
excerpts.note: Ordinance No. 207 — see documents/lah-1886-01-15 for its text, and handbook/MINUTES-TO-CHECK.md for the meeting to pull.

title: Ordinance No. 207, “An Ordinance changing the names of certain streets” — adopted Jan. 6, 1886, approved Jan. 14, published in the Los Angeles Herald Jan. 15, 1886

excerpts.text: An Ordinance changing the names of certain streets.
SECTION 1. That the name of that certain street known as Elm street, and extending from Pico street to California street, be and the same is hereby changed to Olive street.
SECTION 2. That the name of that certain street known as William street, situated in the Childs Tract, be and the same is hereby changed to Santee street.
excerpts.note: ★ The `william` of documents/mr006-378, six months after that sheet was recorded.

excerpts.text: SECTION 3. That the name of that certain street known as William street, and situated in the Los Angeles Improvement Company's subdivision of lots be as the same is hereby changed to Goss street.
excerpts.note: The second William Street. The ordinance exists to tell them apart.

excerpts.text: SECTION 4. The Clerk of the Council shall certify to the passage of this ordinance and shall cause the same to be published once in the Los Angeles DAILY HERALD, and thereupon and thereafter it shall take effect and be in force.

I hereby certify that the foregoing ordinance was adopted by the Council of the city of Los Angeles at its meeting of January 6th, A. D. 1886. W. W. ROBINSON, Clerk of the Council of the City of Los Angeles. Approved this 14th day of January, A. D. 1886. E. F. SPENCE, Mayor.

title: Los Angeles Herald, July 20, 1886, p. 5 — an ordinance changing Guadalupe Street to Davies Street and Cemetery Avenue to Castelar Street is adopted

excerpts.text: Presented an ordinance changing the name of Guadalupe street to Davies street, and name of Cemetery avenue to Castelar street. Adopted.

title: Ordinance No. 242, “An ordinance changing the names of certain streets” — adopted July 19, 1886, approved July 22, published in the Los Angeles Herald July 23, 1886

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the names of certain streets.
SECTION 1. The name of that certain street, extending from Alameda street to Geary street and known as Guadalupe street, be and the same is hereby changed to Davies street.
SEC. 2. The name of that certain street, extending from Temple street to Bellevue avenue and known as Cemetery avenue, be and the same is hereby changed to Castelar street.

I hereby certify that the foregoing ordinance was adopted by the Council of the city of Los Angeles at its meeting of July 19th, A. D., 1886. W. W. ROBINSON, Clerk of the Council of the City of Los Angeles. Approved this 22nd day of July, A. D. 1886. E. F. SPENCE, Mayor.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Sept. 21, 1886, p. 5 — an ordinance changing the name of High Street to Walters Street is adopted

excerpts.text: Presented an ordinance changing name of High street to Walters street. Adopted.

rows.note: The Herald reports the ordinance presented and adopted in one item; the ordinance number and the council day are not in the excerpt. Walters lasted four years — the Oct. 1890 omnibus renaming (lah-1890-10-28) made it Ord Street.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Jan. 4, 1887, p. 7 — an ordinance changing the name of Texas Street to Belmont Avenue is adopted

excerpts.text: The City Attorney presented an ordinance changing the name of Texas street to Belmont avenue. Ordinance adopted.

title: Los Angeles Herald, June 7, 1887, p. 8 — the Board of Public Works recommends that Deep Water Street be renamed Bartlett Street from Beaudry Avenue to Philadelphia Street

excerpts.text: On the petition of R. A. Brown et al., to have Deep Water street changed to Bartlett street, recommend that the City Attorney draft an ordinance changing its name to Bartlett street from Beaudry avenue to Philadelphia street. Adopted.
excerpts.note: "Adopted" is the Council adopting the Board's recommendation, not an ordinance.

title: Los Angeles Herald, June 14, 1887, p. 2 — the Deep Water → Bartlett ordinance is adopted; an ordinance changing Ozier Lane to Winston Street is postponed

excerpts.text: The City Attorney presented an ordinance changing the name of Deep Water street to Bartlett street. Adopted.
A resolution for the improvement of Grand avenue between Eighth and Jefferson streets. Adopted.
excerpts.note: Kept only because it dates Grand Avenue running that far south in 1887.

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the name of Ozier Lane to Winston street. Action postponed.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Jan. 4, 1888, p. 2 — an ordinance changing Le Convieur Street to Ashland Street is read and referred to the special committee on names of streets

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the name of Le Convieur street to Ashland street was read and referred to the special committee on names of streets.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Jan. 24, 1888, p. 2 — the motion to adopt the ordinance changing Locouorer (Le Convieur) Street to Ashland Street is lost, 8 to 5

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the name of Locouorer street to that of Ashland street was read. A motion to adopt it was lost by a vote of eight to five.
excerpts.note: "Locouorer" for Le Convieur — see documents/lah-1888-01-04 for the other spelling.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Oct. 11, 1888, p. 3 — “Street Names. Good Work by a Committee of the Council. Order Brought from Chaos.” The special committee's summary of its 199 proposed changes

excerpts.text: For the past six or eight months a special committee of the City Council has been at work endeavoring to arrange the names of the streets in this city, so that there shall be no two streets of the same name, and that each street shall have a continuous name throughout. This committee is now ready to report, and the ordinance changing the names will probably be passed at the meeting of the Council on Monday. Following is a summary of the changes to be adopted:
excerpts.note: The two purposes stated together — no duplicates, and one name per continuous street. Ordinance No. 48's title six months later keeps only the second. The list executes them in that order: consolidations first, then the duplicate cull alphabetically.

excerpts.text: STREET NAMES. Good Work by a Committee of the Council. ORDER BROUGHT FROM CHAOS. Thoroughfares That Have Had Several Names, Given One Throughout.
The Committee asks that if any further changes are to be suggested, they be made before the next meeting of the Council.
excerpts.note: The document's own statement that it is provisional. Six months and an ordinance later, several of its lines had changed or vanished.

excerpts.text: Botiller St. and Santee St., changed to Martin St.
excerpts.note: ⚠ Did not hold. See documents/lah-1892-01-23, where Martin and Botiller are being changed TO Santee four years later.

excerpts.text: Earl St. and San Julian Ave., changed to San Julian St.
excerpts.note: The absorption research-leads.md logged as undated: the Moran Tract of 1887 letters Earl north of Ninth and San Julian south of it. Item 71 four lines later sends a SECOND street to San Julian — “Myrtle Ave., S. of E. Pico” — so the name was being assembled out of three pieces at once.

excerpts.text: Maple Ave. and Los Angeles St.: from Washington St. south, changed to Regent St.
excerpts.note: ⚠ The reverse of what happened. Ordinance No. 482 of Dec. 1889 changes Regent Street to Maple Avenue.

excerpts.text: Morgan Lane and Mayo St., changed to Mayo St.
excerpts.note: Both names live at once in 1888 — the Orchard Tract's Morgan Lane (documents/mr005-005) and the Mayo Street ordered in Oct. 1883 (documents/lah-1883-10-21).

excerpts.text: Nevada St., Bennett St. and Nevada St., between Ninth and Tenth Sts., changed to Georgia Bell St.
excerpts.note: ★ Corrected against the full-size clip: the middle name is BENNETT, not a third Nevada. The earlier column-scale reading printed “Nevada St., Nevada St. and Nevada St.”, which was a misread. So it is two Nevadas and a Bennett folded into Georgia Bell — still exactly the act names.js describes, and still the reason Forman dated the Georgia Bell renaming to 1889, but the third street had a name of its own.

excerpts.text: Third St. from San Pedro to Wolfskill Ave. and Georgia St., changed to Atchison St.
Aztec Ave. changed to Girard St.
excerpts.note: ⚠ Kines has Aztec Avenue becoming Belmont Avenue. A third account is in documents/lah-1887-01-04, where Texas Street becomes Belmont. None of the three is settled — and item 85 below adds a fourth wrinkle by moving BELMONT itself.

excerpts.text: Belmont Ave., from Pico to Eleventh St., changed to Trenton St.
excerpts.note: ★ New in the full reading, and it bears on the Aztec/Belmont tangle above: in Oct. 1888 Belmont Avenue ran far enough south to reach Pico and Eleventh, and the committee wanted that southern tail taken off it. See `belmont-kincaid`.

excerpts.text: Castellar St., changed to Hill St.
excerpts.note: Proposed in 1888; a portion of Castelar Street actually becomes Hill Street in July 1894 (documents/lah-1894-07-24). Six years between the proposal and the act. (The old column-scale reading printed “Castellar Ave.”; the clip reads St.)

excerpts.text: Elm St. changed to Olive St.
excerpts.note: Already done by Ordinance No. 207 in Jan. 1886 (documents/lah-1886-01-15) — either a different Elm, or the committee listing a change that had already been made.

excerpts.text: Cumberland Ave. and Laura St., changed to Boston St.
excerpts.note: A Laura Street, two years before the Nov. 1889 numbering ordinance turns "Laurel and Adele" into Fifteenth Street. Whether either is the "(formerly Laura St)" of the 1893 Miguel Subdivision is unsettled.

excerpts.text: Beaudry Ave., from Third St. north, changed to Canal St.
excerpts.note: ★★ A DOCUMENTED Beaudry → Canal renaming, and the first source in this corpus that names the pair. `canal-street-beaudry` had to infer the connection from the Canal and Reservoir Company; here the council is proposing the swap outright. ⚠ But note the direction and the date: the Chadwick Subdivision of Dec. 1886 (documents/mr016-059) ALREADY letters Canal Street on that ground, two years before this proposal. So either the committee is regularising a change the subdividers had already made, or Canal was on part of the line and Beaudry on the rest. The two rows are 300 m apart and both north of Third.

excerpts.text: Branch of Beaudry Ave., passing west of Sisters' Hospital, changed to West Canal St.
excerpts.note: ★ The same branch turns up again nine years later, still unresolved: in Dec. 1897 the city engineer reports that “West Beaudry avenue, that part of which is bounded on the west by block 33, Angeleno Heights, and on the east by the Sisters' hospital, should be changed to SUNSET BOULEVARD; this change has hitherto been overlooked” (documents/lah-1897-12-07). Sisters' Hospital fixes the same stretch of ground both times. So this branch was proposed as West Canal in 1888, was still called West Beaudry in 1897, and became Sunset. The 1888 proposal did not hold.

excerpts.text: Crescent Ave., changed to Beaudry St.
excerpts.note: ★★ THE SUCCESSOR TO `crescent-park-tract`, which until now had none. Crescent Avenue is lettered on Prudent Beaudry's own Park tract (documents/mr007-026-p1) — the sheet that letters BOTH Beaudry names on two parallel roadways — and in Oct. 1888 the committee proposes folding Crescent into Beaudry Street. ⚠ WHICH Beaudry matters: this corpus splits `beaudry-st` (the Fremont Avenue lineage) from `beaudry-avenue` by the ink, and the committee writes “Beaudry St.” Whether the Park Tract's Crescent sits on the Fremont line or the Beaudry Avenue line is a geometry question this excerpt makes worth asking.

excerpts.text: Virginia St., in SW. part of city, changed to Rouland St.
excerpts.note: ★ Both names are lettered on the SAME TWO SHEETS — Wright's Subdivision of Jan. 1884 (documents/mr005-431) and the Harvey Tract of 1886 (documents/mr010-077) — as two different streets. So in 1888 the committee is extending an existing neighbouring name over a Virginia rather than coining one. See `rouland-street` and `virginia-conv-center`.

excerpts.text: Virginia St., in W. part of city, changed to Toluca St.
excerpts.note: ★ The Angeleno Heights Virginia. Kines's Toluca page says this was “one of several called ‘Virginia’” before the duplicate cull; here is the cull itself, with all four Virginias in one place — Boyle Heights keeps the name, the SE one becomes Lion, the SW one Rouland, the W one Toluca. See `virginia-st-angeleno-hgts`.

excerpts.text: Warren St., in S. part of city, changed to Decatur St.
excerpts.note: ★★ THIS SOURCES A RENAMING THE CORPUS HAD ONLY FROM ALIGNMENT. `warren-st-arts-district` inferred Warren → Decatur from the fact that the E. B. Millar Tract of 1887 letters Warren on the corridor that Tract No. 1836 letters Decatur in 1913, and said so explicitly: “That is from the alignment, not from a source; no renaming document has been found.” One has now, and it dates the proposal to Oct. 1888 — eighteen months after the Millar tract was recorded, not twenty-six years.

excerpts.text: Jackson St. and Weill St., changed to Sepulveda St.
excerpts.note: ★ The fate of `weill`, which the corpus had lost track of entirely (“The name is gone from Los Angeles”). It went to Sepulveda, folded together with a Jackson Street, in the Oct. 1888 cull.

excerpts.text: Cedar St., in A. Weill tract, changed to Hemlock St.
excerpts.note: ★★ AN INITIAL AND A TRACT. `weill`'s entry says “no Weill of that quarter has been identified” and graded the search `extensive`. This line gives A. WEILL a recorded subdivision of his own in Los Angeles by 1888 — which is a filing in the County map books with his full name in the title block, and the first hard handle on the man.

excerpts.text: Consuelo St. changed to California St.
excerpts.note: ★★ THIS CLOSES A CHAIN. `consuelo` records that the numbering ordinance of Nov. 1889 folded “California, Consuelo, Greenwell and Vejar” into Fourteenth Street, which read as four parallel names going into one number. It was a SEQUENCE: Consuelo became California here in Oct. 1888, and California became Fourteenth thirteen months later. See also `california-street-14th`.

excerpts.text: Cummings Ave., in Angeleño Heights, changed to Modoc St.
excerpts.note: ⚠ CONFLICTS WITH THE PRESERVATION PLAN, which says Hall and Stilson renamed “Cummings to Ionia” for the Hall family's Michigan hometown. Both cannot be the same event. The likeliest reading is that they are two: Hall and Stilson's private renaming on their own tract (1886, per `cummings-ave`), and the city committee's proposal two years later which — since no Modoc Street exists in Angeleno Heights — did not hold. But the plan gives no date for the Ionia change, so the order is not proven.

excerpts.text: La Fayett Ave. in W part of city, changed to Contra Costa St.
excerpts.note: ⚠ A PROPOSAL THAT LOST. The spelling is the paper's. This is `lafayette-bixel` — the west-side Lafayette on what is now Bixel Street, lettered “Lafayette Av.” on the Crown Hill sheet of Nov. 1884 (documents/mr006-115). There is no Contra Costa Street in Los Angeles; the corridor took BIXEL the following year instead. Useful precisely because it fails: it shows the committee choosing California county names by the handful (Tulare, Merced, Solano, Yolo, Napa, Sonoma, Amador, Colusa, Placer, Mono, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Siskiyou, Stanislaus, San Joaquin, Del Norte in this list alone) and losing some of them to the ground.

excerpts.text: Fudickar or Fudigar St., in W. part of city, changed to King St.
excerpts.note: A street with two spellings at once, and the committee prints both. ⚠ The proposal half-held and then reversed: in Dec. 1897 the city engineer is still calling it Fudigar and proposing “Fudigar street, Temple to Bellevue, changed to Sugg street”, while a DIFFERENT King Street, First to Temple, is to become Sugg as well (documents/lah-1897-12-07). Nine years on, both names are still in play.

excerpts.text: Sainsevain St., changed to Commercial St.
excerpts.note: ★ The Sainsevain of the Aliso vineyard circle — Pedro Sainsevain, Vignes's nephew — losing his street to a generic. Frenchtown Confidential's description of Labory Lane puts it “east of the Southern Pacific tracks to Lafayette”, in this same quarter, and the Huntington's Solano-Reeve record for the Alanis Vineyard Tract runs “Sainsevain St. to Labory Lane”. See `labory-lane`.

excerpts.text: Huber St., in Bliss tract, changed to Mendocino St.
excerpts.note: The Bliss tract, which the Herald of Oct. 19, 1886 places “on E side Alameda street” in a decree quieting title for Oliver H. Bliss against the Wolfskill heirs. Not yet a name in this corpus; recorded here because the tract is now doubly attested.

excerpts.text: Fuller St., changed to Glowner St.
excerpts.note: ★ Where Glowner Street comes from. Nine years later the engineer proposes to take it away again — “Glowner street, Twenty-second to Twenty-fifth street, changed to Wall street” (documents/lah-1897-12-07) — so the name lasted about a decade and this is its birth certificate.

excerpts.text: Agate Ave., and Koster St., changed to Agate st. / Koster Ave., changed to Koster St.
excerpts.note: Two consecutive items, quoted together because they only make sense as a pair: the committee takes the name Koster off one street and puts it on another, so that Agate and Koster each end up on one line instead of crossing. A clean worked example of what “given one throughout” meant in practice.

title: Los Angeles Herald, “Broadway — Fort Street Is No Longer in Existence,” Feb. 20, 1890 (the renaming ordinance signed by Mayor Hazard and in effect)

excerpts.text: BROADWAY. Fort Street Is No Longer in Existence.
There is no longer a Fort street in Los Angeles. The ordinance changing its name to Broadway has gone into effect, having been signed by Mayor Hazard and published as required by law.

It is hinted that in a short time a part of Main street, from Tenth street south, will be called Broadway. This it is said will be done as soon as Broadway is extended. An examination of the city map will show that Main street makes a bend at Seventh street, and that when Broadway is cut through that portion south of Tenth street will be nearly in a straight line with Broadway. Parties now living on the lower part of Main street may make up their minds to announce that they will reside on Broadway.
excerpts.note: A prediction, and it gets no row: “it is hinted” and “it is said” are not an instrument. Kept because it is the earliest account of why Broadway runs where it does south of downtown, and because whatever later act carried it out is now a thing to look for.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Nov. 9, 1890, p. 5 — “The Old Names Best”: Mayor Hazard returns the street-renaming ordinance unsigned

excerpts.text: THE OLD NAMES BEST. A Street By Any Other Name Will Not Be So Well Known.

The mayor filed a message with the city clerk yesterday for presentation to the council on Monday, returning unsigned the ordinance "changing the names of certain streets and avenues in the city of Los Angeles." Mayor Hazard does not approve of continually changing the names of old established streets, and thinks that under no circumstances should a change be made except when one continued street is called by two names in different parts. He deprecates the practice that has obtained under the present administration of changing the familiar names without any apparent reason, thereby bewildering everybody.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Nov. 11, 1890, p. 3 — the mayor's veto message is read and the ordinance referred back to the Board of Public Works for amendment; Major Bonsall defends the changes

Stephenson avenue, for instance, had been suggested in open council as a better name for the east portion of Second street, because of its deflection to the south in Boyle Heights. Another instance where changes were necessary was that of Water, Waters and Walters streets, which were so much alike as to be confusing. In any event the board had not acted upon its own accord, but had made the changes in accordance with the wishes of the property owners, as expressed in petitions to the council.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Feb. 5, 1897, p. 5 — “It Is Not Satisfactory”: protests against the street-naming ordinance, and Major Horace Bell's own account of how Georgia Bell Street got its name

excerpts.text: IT IS NOT SATISFACTORY. The ordinance changing the names of streets, as passed by the council and recommended by the commission appointed for that purpose, has raised quite a storm of protests, and the document will probably be returned to the council without the executive's signature. Mayor Snyder's life has been made a burden to him ever since the ordinance passed, listening to complaints, and he has about made up his mind not to approve it. There is a very general objection to the many Spanish names introduced, the objection being urged that they are exceedingly difficult to pronounce and are in many instances unwieldy.

One of the strongest protestants is Major Horace Bell, who insists that General Forman, one of the commissioners, has taken advantage of his position to "get even on him." His specific complaint is against the changing of the name of Georgia Bell street to Nevada street. He says that when he laid out his subdivision, he gave a number of streets to the city, and among them named one Georgia and another Virginia, for his wife and daughter, respectively. Later it was found that there was another Georgia street, and Bell was added to his street. Gen. Forman, he says, later laid out a subdivision north of him and gave the connecting street with Georgia Bell the name of Nevada. He also had the name of Virginia street named DeLong, in honor of a mining man.
excerpts.note: ★ The naming of Georgia Bell Street, from the man who did it.

excerpts.text: Later the council changed the name of Nevada street to Georgia Bell to make it uniform. This was some years ago, and now the commission has changed the name of the entire street back to Nevada, which, Major Bell says, is on account of personal feeling. It is also understood that the mayor is dissatisfied with the innovation of calling streets "ways" in the northeastern part of the city. It is probable that the mayor will send a message to the council setting forth his views at length, and giving his objections in detail.
excerpts.note: "To make it uniform" is Ordinance No. 48, in force May 10, 1889.

The mayor gives his reason for his action at some length, his principal objections being the adoption of a number of Spanish names, which, he says, would be difficult for newcomers to spell or pronounce, and the further fact of the large number of protests from the East side, presumably against the innovation in designating streets in that section as "ways."

It is to be hoped that the differences can be satisfactorily adjusted on Monday next, to which time the hearing was continued. The commissioners certainly labored faithfully and put in six weeks hard work, without compensation, in straightening out the tangled maze of duplicate names and misnomers in our street nomenclature, a fact which should at least be appreciated by their fellow citizens, and it would be a pity to have this work lost. This has been the first systematic attempt to properly name the streets of the city, and there is no doubt that if the protestants will only be reasonable, the differences can be adjusted and an ordinance adopted that will be generally satisfactory. The commissioners certainly have no personal axes to grind, and they should be met in the same spirit which prompted them to undertake their arduous and thankless task.
