title: Los Angeles Herald, Feb. 24, 1897, p. 4 — the council passes the street-naming ordinance as amended by the joint committee; the Georgia Bell–Nevada tangle is compromised by naming the street Georgia

excerpts.text: The city council yesterday passed the ordinance changing street names as amended in line with the report of the joint committee, printed in The Herald Sunday morning, with but one or two unimportant changes. A compromise on the Georgia Bell-Nevada street tangle was reached by naming that thoroughfare Georgia street. There was much argument over the matter, but personalities were barred. It is possible that an effort will be made to take the matter into court.
excerpts.note: ★ "printed in The Herald Sunday morning" — Feb. 21, 1897, the joint committee's amendment list. Wanted.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Feb. 27, 1897, p. 3 — “Signed the Ordinance”: Mayor Snyder signs the street-naming ordinance and it becomes law; Major Bell will not go to court

excerpts.text: Signed the Ordinance. Mayor Snyder yesterday signed the ordinance changing and revising street names, as passed by the council at the last meeting, and it is now the law. Major Horace Bell, while not satisfied with the name Georgia street, will not take the case into the courts, as he at first declared he would, and there will now be no further trouble over the matter.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Oct. 26, 1897 — “Street Naming”: the city engineer asks to be authorized to gather all needed changes into one ordinance, and reports a list open to inspection in his office

excerpts.text: Street Naming. The city engineer, to whom had been referred the matter of changing the names of certain streets, submitted the following report, which was referred to the board of public works with instructions to examine the maps referred to: "In regard to your order to present an ordinance changing the names of certain streets, I would respectfully state that there are a number of other streets in the city whose names need changing, and for the purpose of avoiding confusion I would recommend that this office be authorized to include all these streets in one ordinance. There is a list of these streets open to inspection in this office."
excerpts.note: ★ A working list of streets needing renaming, in the City Engineer's office in 1897.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Dec. 7, 1897 — the city engineer's omnibus report: Sixth Street from Hoover to the west city boundary to become Wilshire Boulevard, Glowner Street to become Wall Street, and some thirty other changes, each with its reason

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the names of the following streets was referred to the board of public works: Ward street from Hoover to Bautista, changed to Sixth street; Gante street changed to Elwood street; Jewel street, Sapphire street to north termination, changed to Bixel street; Sixth street, Hoover street to west city boundary, changed to Wilshire boulevard; Glowner street, Twenty-second to Twenty-fifth street, changed to Wall street; Jaurez street changed to Jasmine street; Killarney street changed to King street, Bidwell street changed to Sixteenth street; King street, First to Temple street changed to Sugg street; Fudigar street, Temple to Bellevue, changed to Sugg street.
excerpts.note: ★ Wilshire Boulevard, and Wall Street reaching Twenty-fifth.

excerpts.text: In regard to your order to present an ordinance changing the name of De Celis street to Woodlawn avenue, the city engineer finds that there is already a Woodlawn street in existence. He suggests that the name De Celis street be changed to Main street, and that the name of that portion of Main street lying south of the junction of Main and De Celis streets be changed to such other name as the council may see fit. The house-numbering system for that section of the city was designed with the idea that De Celis street would be changed to Main street. Referred to the board of public works.
excerpts.note: The Main Street tangle again — compare the Moneta Avenue difficulty of Mar. 1899 (documents/lah-1899-03-14).

excerpts.text: Ninth street, from Vermont avenue westerly, as shown on the Electric Railway Homestead Association tract, should be changed to South Marino street, for the reason that there are now two names for this straight street. Clermont avenue, from Washington street to McNally street, should be changed to Cimmaron street, for the reason that there are now two names. Juliet avenue, from Twenty-second street to Adams street, should be changed to Juliet street, to conform with Juliet street south of Adams. Clifton avenue, from Clifton street to its northerly termination, should be changed to Clifton street. Alvira street, from Rosedale to Bonita in the Turner tract, should be changed to Twenty-fourth street; reason, the north half is called Alvira street and the south half is known as Twenty-fourth street. West Beaudry avenue, that part of which is bounded on the west by block 33, Angeleno Heights, and on the east by the Sisters' hospital, should be changed to Sunset boulevard; this change has hitherto been overlooked. Cambridge avenue, from Western avenue to Pellissier street, in the Washington-street and Pico-street Heights tract, should be changed to Cambridge street; it is now known both as street and avenue. Violet street, from Rosedale to Bonita in the Turner tract, should be changed to Twenty-third street. Primrose avenue, formerly Iliad street in the How tract, should be changed to Avenue 28. Ella street, in the Highland View tract, should be changed to Avenue 37. Bellard street, in the Washington-street tract, should be changed to Stanford avenue. Church street, in the Central Park Front tract, should be changed to Zamora street. Church street, in Old Clapp Orchard, should be changed to Zamora street.
excerpts.note: Every entry carries its diagnosis. Note the Sunset Boulevard gap-filling four years after documents/lah-1893-10-29 assembled it.

excerpts.text: Castello street, in the Anderson tract, should be changed to Zamora street. Herbert street, in the Lienaus Cottage Home tract, should be changed to Thirty-sixth street. Harwood street, in the Harwood tract, should be changed to Fifty-seventh street. San Diego street, from Santa Monica avenue to Figueroa street, should be changed; I would suggest to Rosecrans way. Park street, in Lambies subdivision, should be changed to San Pablo street. Alturas street, formerly Prospect street, in the Norton tract, should be changed; I would suggest Walker street. That portion of San Fernando street which was formerly Olympia street, should be changed to Downey avenue, as there are now two branches of San Fernando. Juanita street in Maltman's first addition should be changed to Juanita avenue. Rocksbury street in Kurts & Bradshaw's sub should be changed to Roxbury avenue. Basil street should be changed to ——
excerpts.note: The tail of the column, supplied 2026-09-17. ★ THREE THINGS IN IT are worth more than the renamings. (1) The engineer twice writes “I WOULD SUGGEST” — Rosecrans way, Walker street — which is him coining a name at his desk rather than reporting one in use, exactly the hazard handbook/change-rows-amendment.md §10 form 5 was written about, and here the document itself marks which lines those are. (2) “Alturas street, FORMERLY PROSPECT STREET, in the Norton tract” closes a loop with documents/lah-1888-10-11, which proposed “Prospect St., in Norton tract, changed to Altemas St.” nine years earlier — so the 1888 committee's ALTEMAS was carried out and then drifted, in print at least, to ALTURAS. (3) “Castello street, in the ANDERSON tract” is a third sighting of an Anderson holding; see the header. ⚠ The last line is cut off by the bottom of the crop: what Basil Street was to become is not known from this clip.

excerpts.text: Naud street. Referred to board of public works.
excerpts.note: The second clip: a fragment from further down the same column, after the engineer's report. The rest of the item is off the crop, so what was being referred about Naud Street is not known.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Dec. 28, 1897 — grade ordinances for Albion Street and Twenty-fifth Street, and an ordinance changing the names of certain streets

excerpts.text: Changing and establishing the grade of Albion street, between Avenue 18 and Main street; also establishing the grade of Twentyfifth street from a point 299.8 feet east of Rosedale avenue to a point 135 feet west of Leoti avenue; also ordinance changing the names of certain streets.
excerpts.note: "Avenue 18" in use by Dec. 1897 — the numbered-avenue system of documents/lah-1896-05-16.

title: Los Angeles Herald, May 28, 1898 — board of public works refers Samuel Mansfield's petition to change Niza street to Lee avenue

excerpts.text: All the members of the board of public works were present yesterday at the regular weekly meeting. The board recommended that the petition from Samuel Mansfield be referred to the city engineer with instructions to present the necessary ordinance changing the name of Niza street to Lee avenue.
excerpts.note: Asked only. Named petitioner: Samuel Mansfield.

title: Los Angeles Herald, June 12, 1898 — board of public works recommends folding Mission road and part of Bauchet street into Mission boulevard

excerpts.text: The board of public works recommends that the city engineer be instructed to prepare an ordinance changing the name of Mission road, between the northwest corner of the Arroyo de los Posas subdivision and the east city line to Mission boulevard; also changing the name of Bauchet street, between the east line of the Bauchet tract and the easterly line of lot 43 of the Bauchet tract, to Mission boulevard.
excerpts.note: Both extents are stated by tract boundary rather than by cross street.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Aug. 2, 1898 — ordinance passed changing Bullard street to Court street and Rosedale avenue to Normandie avenue

excerpts.text: The following ordinances were presented and passed: Final ordinance for establishing the grade of Santee street from Eighth to the widow Botiller tract; ordinance of intention for the construction of sewer on Soto street from First to Second and on Palmetto street from Alameda to Mateo; ordinance permitting the property owners of Orchard avenue between Thirtieth to Jefferson to improve said street by private contract; ordinance changing the names of Bullard street and Rosedale avenue to Court street and Normandie avenue respectively.
excerpts.note: "The widow Botiller tract" is our Widow Botiller Tract (see names.js botiller-street). "Mateo" here is post-Molino Mateo — cf. documents/min-1896-08-31.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Nov. 8, 1898 — ordinance adopted changing Delgado street to Cecilia street

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the name of Delgado street to Cecilia street was adopted.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Nov. 29, 1898 — E. V. Baker asks that Yolande street become West Thirtieth; the council orders Thirtieth Place instead, and Covarrubias street to Effie street

excerpts.text: In the matter of the petition of E. V. Baker, asking that the name of Yolande street be changed to West Thirtieth, on the recommendation of the board of public works the city engineer was directed to prepare an ordinance changing the name of the street to Thirtieth Place; also one changing the name of Covarrubias street to Effie street.
excerpts.note: Petitioner asked for West Thirtieth; council ordered Thirtieth Place. Named petitioner: E. V. Baker.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Mar. 14, 1899 — "Change of Street Names: Difficulties Arising Over Renaming of Moneta Avenue"

excerpts.text: The city attorney reported in the matter of the instructions received by him to present an ordinance changing the name of Moneta avenue back to Main street, that this proceeding will necessitate a new name for what is now known as Main street. The attorney also called attention to the fact that the house numbering system in the southern addition is planned on the basis of Main street as it is now called, and any change in the street names, as proposed, will result in confusion, and recommended that the name of Stanley avenue be changed to San Pedro street, and that the name of that portion of San Pedro street south of Stanley avenue be changed to such name as desired. This last is desirable for the purpose of maintaining uniformity in the direction of the main streets running in northerly and southerly directions.
excerpts.note: "Changing the name of Moneta avenue BACK to Main street" implies an earlier Main-to-Moneta change we have not yet found.

excerpts.text: The entire matter was referred to the board of public works for investigation and recommendation.

title: Los Angeles Herald, May 6, 1899 — board recommends reversing the names of Mission Road and Alhambra avenue; Councilman Pierce objects

excerpts.text: It was decided to recommend that the city engineer be instructed to present an ordinance changing and reversing the names of Mission Road and Alhambra avenue from the intersection at Eastlake park to the city limits. Councilman Pierce is very much opposed to giving Alhambra avenue the name Mission Road, which has been in existence fifty years.
excerpts.note: A name SWAP over a shared extent, not two independent changes.

title: Los Angeles Herald, June 28, 1899 — ordinance changing Concord Court to Green street read for the first time

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the name of Concord Court to Green street was read for the first time.

title: Los Angeles Herald, July 26, 1899 — Pasadena board of public works recommends six street-name changes

excerpts.text: The board has had under consideration for some time the change of the names of several streets and avenues. The following changes are recommended: Arlington court to Arlington drive. Central street to Ritzman street. Locust street to Holly street. Union avenue to Manzanita avenue. West Columbia street and Hill street, which connects West Columbia and Columbia, to Columbia street. San Pasqual street between Fair Oaks and Marengo street to Pico street.
excerpts.note: Pasadena. Five of the six recur in documents/lah-1899-10-11 as passed.

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the name of [?]tle avenue to Broadway was passed.
excerpts.note: The old name is illegible in the clip — one or two characters lost at the column edge before "tle avenue". Not transcribable from this scan.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Aug. 9, 1899 — an ordinance changing the names of certain streets, as heretofore published, ordered drawn

excerpts.text: An ordinance changing the names of certain streets, as heretofore published, was ordered drawn, and an investigation of the building certain sheds in violation of the directions of the council was ordered made.
excerpts.note: "As heretofore published" — the list exists in print BEFORE the ordinance. Step 2b.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Oct. 11, 1899 — Pasadena passes the street-name ordinance, dropping the Congress street change; the older street keeps the name

excerpts.text: The ordinance changing the names of various streets was passed as first read, with the omission of the change in the name of Congress street, between Fair Oaks and Pasadena avenue. There are two Congress streets, one between Fair Oaks and Pasadena avenue and the other between St. John's street and Orange Grove. The residents of the latter street petitioned the council to change the name of the former for their convenience. The council decided that since the former street was the first to receive the name it was entitled to retain it over the other street.
excerpts.note: SENIORITY RULE: the street that got the name first keeps it.

excerpts.text: In accordance with the ordinance passed, Arlington court will hereafter be called Arlington drive. Central street will be known now as Ritzman, to avoid confusion with Center street. Locust street, between Fair Oaks and Raymond, will be called Holly, there being another Locust street on the East Side. The name of Union avenue has been changed to Manzanita avenue, to be distinguished from Union street. West Columbia and Hill street are now named Columbia. There have been two San Pasqual streets, one on the East Side and another between South Fair Oaks and Marengo avenues.
excerpts.note: The excerpt ends at a full stop, not a truncation. Every stated MOTIVE here is duplicate-avoidance.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Jan. 6, 1900 — Garvanza renaming and renumbering ordinance recommended for passage without amendment

excerpts.text: The ordinance changing, re-naming and renumbering the streets of Garvanza district was recommended for passage without amendment, the anticipated opposition to the change from some of the residents failing to develop, no one opposing the improvement.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Jan. 9, 1900 — the Garvanza renaming and renumbering ordinance passed without comment

excerpts.text: The ordinance changing the names and numberings of that portion of the Garvanza district recently annexed, to conform to the streets of the city, was passed upon reading without comment, the matter having been previously fully discussed before the board of public works.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Oct. 23, 1900 — city engineer presents an ordinance changing Leahy street to Sacramento street

excerpts.text: In his report the city engineer stated that he presented final ordinance for the repaving of Eleventh street, from Main to Hope; also final ordinance establishing grade of Catalina street, from Pico to Eleventh; also, an ordinance changing name of Leahy street to Sacramento street; also furnished freeholders with correct city boundary lines. The engineer called the attention of the council to the condition of the box storm drain or sewer at the northeast corner of Fourth and Los Angeles streets, which he declared a nuisance and of no service to the city. The report was approved.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Mar. 13, 1901 — ordinance passed changing West street to Pacific avenue

excerpts.text: The city council at its last meeting passed an ordinance changing the name of West street to Pacific avenue.
excerpts.note: "At its last meeting" — the council date is before Mar. 13, 1901, not Mar. 13.

title: Los Angeles Herald, July 31, 1901 — ordinance changing the names of several streets read for the first time; a further proposition referred to the committee on streets and alleys

excerpts.text: City Attorney Willett presented the draft of the ordinance regulating street elevations; the ordinance changing the names of several streets was read for the first time, and upon recommendation of Councilman Reynolds, the proposition to change the names of several other streets and alleys was referred to the committee on streets and alleys; the diagram presented by the city engineer for the construction of a sewer in Pasadena avenue, and several other thoroughfares was approved by the board;
excerpts.note: ALLEYS as well as streets — the only mention of alley renaming in the run.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Aug. 7, 1901 — ordinance adopted changing Colorado Court to North Grand avenue

excerpts.text: passed; the ordinance changing the name of Colorado Court to North Grand avenue was adopted; the resolution approving the city engineer's diagram
excerpts.note: Clip begins and ends mid-sentence.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Feb. 17, 1903 — ordinance adopted changing East Jefferson street, Virginia street or Thirtieth street, between Eureka street and Central avenue, to Thirty-eighth street

excerpts.text: from Ninth to Seventh streets. Adopting an ordinance changing and establishing the name of East Jefferson street, Virginia street or Thirtieth street, between Eureka street and Central avenue, to Thirty-eighth street.
excerpts.note: THREE simultaneous names for one street, resolved to a fourth. Clip begins mid-sentence.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Mar. 14, 1905 — "Street Names Are Changed": five south-side changes passed, four of them renumberings

excerpts.text: Owing to the conflict in the numbering of certain streets in the southern portion of the city the city engineer yesterday requested that the following changes in names be made. Murdock street to Forty-eighth, Woodmen avenue to Forty-ninth, Waco avenue and Waco street to Fiftieth street, Forty-ninth street from Main to Moneta to Forty-eighth street, Fiftieth street from Main to Moneta to Forty-ninth street.
excerpts.note: The last two are renumberings of already-numbered streets over a stated extent.

excerpts.text: The ordinance changing the names of these streets was passed by the council.

title: Los Angeles Herald, May 13, 1905 — "To Change Names of 90 Streets": City Engineer Stafford's system for the Fifth and Sixth wards, passed and awaiting the mayor

excerpts.text: City Engineer Stafford, acting under instructions from the council, has drawn up a new system of naming streets in the southern and southeastern portion of the city, comprising sections of the Fifth and Sixth wards.
excerpts.note: Headline: "To Change Names of 90 Streets / Measure Will Affect Fifth and Sixth Wards / Applies to Cross Streets."

excerpts.text: Many tracts have been laid out from time to time in this section without due attention being paid to the location of the streets, owing to the fact that some of the principal thoroughfares running north and south do not run parallel to each other. Then again, the cross streets have been cut through in sections. For instance, a street would be improved for five blocks, then it would stop to begin again several blocks further on, and repeat.
excerpts.note: The stated cause: tract-by-tract platting with no city-wide grid.

excerpts.text: The ordinance changing the names of ninety of these cross streets was passed last Monday and is now in Mayor McAleer's hands awaiting his decision on the question.
excerpts.note: Passed Monday = May 8, 1905. Recalled from the mayor three days after this — see documents/lah-1905-05-16.

excerpts.text: By the provisions of the ordinance a number of the residents will be moved nearer the center of the city as far as the maps are concerned. For instance, what has been known as Forty-ninth street in a certain section will be changed to Forty-first street.
excerpts.note: The only concrete change named in the article.

excerpts.text: Of course the changing of the names of the streets will change the house numbering materially and necessitate a change on the assessor's, registrar's and tax collector's books, and, in fact, all the books in the city departments where such records are kept. It is also expected that this change in the numbering of houses and of streets will cause the postoffice department considerable trouble for some time to come.
excerpts.note: Assessor's, registrar's and tax collector's books are all named as needing revision — four more record series that would carry the list.

excerpts.text: What will be the mayor's action upon this ordinance is not as yet known, but he will probably sign it or send it back to the council with his reasons in the near future.
excerpts.note: He did neither: the council recalled it first.

title: Los Angeles Herald, May 16, 1905 — the ninety-street ordinance recalled from the mayor by the council

excerpts.text: The ordinance changing the names of ninety streets in the southern portion of the city was recalled from the mayor by the council yesterday.
excerpts.note: "Yesterday" = May 15, 1905.

title: Los Angeles Herald, May 17, 1905 — "Sixth Ward Has a 'Kick' Coming": the protest that stopped the ninety-street ordinance

excerpts.text: City Engineer Stafford says the Sixth ward is out of line with the remainder of the city, that is the streets are. The Sixth warders declare the remainder of the city is out of line with the Sixth ward.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Sixth Ward Has a 'Kick' Coming / Objects Strenuously to Being Moved / City Must Get Into Line."

excerpts.text: Which shall be moved, the Sixth ward or the whole town slid to one side and Eighth street rechristened First, and the lanes between it and the present First streets named Monday boulevard, Tuesday lane, Wednesday place, etc., after the days of the week, or shall a number of the streets in the southern part of the city be rechristened to give the city a uniform system of house numbering?

In pursuance of instructions from the council, the city engineer has been putting forth strenuous efforts to straighten out the streets of the city, and a week ago Monday presented an ordinance changing the numbering or naming of ninety streets in the northern portion of Los Angeles. This ordinance was adopted and sent to the mayor. The people of the Sixth ward felt that they should be consulted in the question and entered a protest. On their request the ordinance was recalled from the mayor by the council and will be reconsidered.
excerpts.note: "Northern" appears to be an error for southern — every other clip says southern, and the Fifth and Sixth wards are southern.

excerpts.text: The city, and particularly the Sixth ward, has had a tremendous growth during the past few years. Many new tracts have been opened, which have rapidly been built up with homes. Owing to the manner in which some of these tracts were laid out, and the fact that some of the old country thoroughfares which ran through them do not run north and south as the other streets of the city leading in the same general direction are supposed to, the streets in the tracts do not fair up with the thoroughfares of the same number on the west side of the city.

With the names of ninety streets changed, the post office would be all out of kilter with the district, and it might take many months and possibly a year or more to get that department entirely straight on the question. The residents of the section dislike going to bed one night on one street and waking up and finding their street has moved six or seven blocks away, leaving them on another.
excerpts.note: From the second clip.

excerpts.text: The council recognizes the right of the residents of the section in question and the whole question will be thoroughly investigated. It is considered likely that the present ordinance will be entirely done away with and some new plan adopted.
excerpts.note: From the second clip. Direct warning against writing rows from the ninety-street ordinance.

title: Los Angeles Herald, May 18, 1905 — "Early Survey Is Cause of Mixup": Lieutenant Hancock's 1849 twenty-eight-degree grid blamed for the whole numbering problem

excerpts.text: The proposed ordinance changing the names of ninety streets in the southern portion of the city affects so many people and such a large district that a great many citizens call every day at the city hall to object to the measure or find out what has been done with it.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Early Survey Is Cause of Mixup / Street Naming a Serious Problem / Systems Are Suggested / Angle Adopted by the City for Running Streets in 1849 Responsible for Discrepancy in Numbers and Names."

excerpts.text: The council has recalled the ordinance, which was passed two weeks ago, and will make some disposition of it next Monday. It is considered probable that no definite action will be taken on the question until Councilman Smith of the First ward returns from his trip of inspection of the property which he owns in the Bullfrog and Goldfield district. Mr. Smith may not return to Los Angeles for another week.
excerpts.note: "Next Monday" = May 22, 1905. That council meeting is the target — see handbook/MINUTES-TO-CHECK.md.

excerpts.text: The change in names affects both the Fifth and Sixth wards. One chief cause of the discrepancy in the numbers of the streets running east and west through the district affected is the fact that Jefferson street runs in a curve instead of in a straight line. Jefferson corresponds to Thirty-fourth street. At Central avenue it ends and runs into Thirty-sixth street and is but two short blocks from Thirty-eighth street.
excerpts.note: Jefferson = Thirty-fourth. Cf. documents/lah-1903-02-17, where "East Jefferson street" between Eureka and Central becomes Thirty-eighth.

excerpts.text: At Figueroa street the condition is entirely different. The way the streets are numbered there are but three blocks between Jefferson at this point and the southern boundary of the old pueblo of Los Angeles. On the west side of Figueroa there are four blocks, Thirty-eighth being on the boundary.

Lieutenant Hancock of the United States engineer corps laid out the pueblo of Los Angeles in 1849 under orders from the city council, and for some reason not now plain, he adopted a system of running his streets on an angle of twenty-eight degrees instead of north and south and east and west. This was done despite the fact that the land lines of the pueblo were run north and south, and comprised an area six miles square.
excerpts.note: ★ The origin of the downtown grid angle, as the city understood it in 1905. Testable against our own geometry.

excerpts.text: The section of the city taken in since the south was laid out on right angles, and all of the streets now running into this section from the city change from their angle and run directly north and south when they reach the boundary line. This causes the mixup. So great is this difference that a person going out Fortieth street from Main finds himself, on crossing Figueroa, to be on Fiftieth street.

City Engineer Stafford and the council are looking for a solution of this problem. Some system of numbering only alternate streets and naming the intervening ones seems to be the solution which has occurred to most of the interested parties, but none wish all of the changes made on one side of the city. They desire that the changes be divided between the wards evenly. This is the view taken by the council and the question will be thoroughly investigated.
excerpts.note: The objection was to the distribution of the burden, not to renaming as such.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Dec. 27, 1907 — Mayor Harper signs a batch of street ordinances, including changes to Reservoir street, Hermosa street and South avenue

excerpts.text: Mayor A. C. Harper yesterday signed a batch of street ordinances that foreshadow a large amount of improvement work. The legal holidays delayed legislation bearing on them.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Mayor Signs Batch of Street Ordinances." "Yesterday" = Dec. 26, 1907.

excerpts.text: Changing the name of Reservoir street.
excerpts.note: Old name only. New name not printed.

excerpts.text: Ordinance changing the name of Hermosa street and South avenue.
excerpts.note: Old names only. New names not printed. Two streets, possibly one ordinance.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Mar. 13, 1908 — Mayor Harper signs the ordinance renaming many streets in the southwestern district

excerpts.text: Mayor Harper yesterday signed the ordinance changing the names of many streets in the southwestern district.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Mayor Signs Ordinance Changing Street Names / Hundreds of House Numbers in the Southwestern District Will Be Altered Next Month by New Measure."

excerpts.text: The new measure differs from what the engineer's department suggested but it has been indorsed by the improvement associations of the Fifth and Sixth wards, hence city officials are satisfied.
excerpts.note: The engineer's draft and the enacted ordinance are DIFFERENT lists.

excerpts.text: Hundreds of house numbers will be changed as well as the street names in thirty days, when the bill becomes effective.
excerpts.note: Effective about Apr. 11, 1908.

title: Los Angeles Herald, July 14, 1908 — "Wilshire Boulevard Would Go It Alone": Wilshire property owners petition to undo the renaming of Orange street

excerpts.text: Wilshire boulevard objects to having Orange street tacked onto it and given the name of Los Angeles' most exclusive residence street, and through an attorney the property owners presented a petition to the city council yesterday asking that the name of Orange street be restored.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Wilshire Boulevard Would Go It Alone / Merger of Orange Street Most Objectionable."

excerpts.text: Two weeks ago the council passed an ordinance changing the name of Orange street, from Figueroa to Alvarado, to Wilshire boulevard. The ordinance was passed on a petition originating among the property owners on Orange street.
excerpts.note: QUALIFIED: Figueroa to Alvarado. Passed about June 30, 1908.

excerpts.text: Yesterday protestants from Wilshire boulevard told the council Orange street could never be a boulevard. According to the protest the street is only sixty feet wide, and the lots so short that the street never could be widened to boulevard size and leave depth enough for the building of residences suitable for a boulevard.
The ordinance changing the name and declaring Orange street a part of Wilshire boulevard will be reconsidered at the council meeting in two weeks.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Sept. 22, 1908 — "Healy Pleads Against Loss of 'Buena Vista'": Fort street, Buena Vista and Downey avenue ordered changed to Broadway

excerpts.text: By a vote of eight to one yesterday the city engineer was instructed to prepare an ordinance changing the name of Fort street, from First to Bellevue, Buena Vista, from Bellevue to the river, and Downey avenue from Avenue Eighteen to Mission road, to Broadway.
excerpts.note: Three QUALIFIED changes to one name. "Yesterday" = Sept. 21, 1908.

excerpts.text: The one negative vote was from Councilman Healy, who instead of favoring changing the name of Buena Vista to Broadway, was in favor of changing all of Broadway to Buena Vista. He thought Buena Vista a much prettier name and every city in the country had its Broadway, while so far as he knew Los Angeles was the only one with its Buena Vista. The old associations and early history of Los Angeles recalled by the name of Buena Vista was another argument he gave for his negative.

Councilman Dromgold, who is responsible for the measure, told the council that Buena Vista would still retain its name from Temple to Bellevue, and it was the only place where the name really fits, as it was high ground on these two blocks and the only place where a "beautiful view" could be had. Downey avenue, he said, would still retain its name from the river to Avenue Eighteen.
excerpts.note: States the REMAINDER extents as well as the changed ones.

excerpts.text: Fort street is that which is now known as North Broadway, from First to the tunnel, but which has never officially been named Broadway.
excerpts.note: ★ A street in common use under a name it did not legally hold.

excerpts.text: The ordinance will be presented by the city engineer as soon as the paving of Downey avenue is completed. It would be inexpedient to change the name before as it would conflict with the Vrooman act, under which the paving is being done.
excerpts.note: ★ A LEGAL reason for delay between decision and ordinance — the Vrooman act (street improvement assessments). Explains gaps elsewhere.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Oct. 27, 1908 — council passes ordinances rearranging portions of Macy, Prospect place, Yosemite, Pennsylvania and Brooklyn into continuous streets

excerpts.text: In order to make several streets as straight as possible much street juggling was done in the council yesterday. Ordinances were passed changing portions of street names.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Council Passes Ordinance Changing Streets' Names." "Yesterday" = Oct. 26, 1908.

excerpts.text: Portions of Macy, Prospect place, Yosemite and Pennsylvania avenue are changed to Bridge street, making Bridge a continuous street to Main. Portions of Brooklyn, Yosemite and Prospect are changed to Pennsylvania and portions of Brooklyn avenue to Prospect place.
excerpts.note: All `extent` scope; no extents given. Yosemite is split between two new names.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Dec. 5, 1908 — "Again Want Name of Street Changed": the Orange-to-Wilshire ordinance repealed, and a new petition for Sunset place

excerpts.text: Several months ago Orange street residents presented a petition to the city council to change the name of Orange street to Wilshire boulevard. The council passed the ordinance and the name was changed. Sign posts were immediately put up designating Orange street as Wilshire boulevard.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Again Want Name of Street Changed / Residents Ask That Orange Be Called Sunset."

excerpts.text: When residents of the exclusive residence street that bears that name learned what had been done they were very indignant at the intrusion on their privacy. A number of them appeared before the city council and protested. They declared Orange street was in no sense a boulevard, that it never could be a boulevard, as a boulevard is understood, that it was built up with apartment houses and nothing but apartment houses would ever be built on it, and altogether it was not such a nice street as the original Wilshire boulevard, and would the council please take it back.
The council did so. The ordinance changing the name of Orange street was repealed and Orange street is still Orange street.
excerpts.note: ★ A repeal. The Wilshire name stood on Orange street roughly July–Dec. 1908.

excerpts.text: Yesterday another petition was filed with the council asking that the name of that portion of Orange street between Hoover and Wilshire boulevard be changed to Sunset place.
excerpts.note: QUALIFIED: Hoover to Wilshire boulevard.

excerpts.text: The petitioners represent this portion of the street has always been known as Sunset place, and, in fact, the property owners believed this to be the real name of the street until signs were posted on the corners calling it Orange street. They further declare the postoffice department knows the street as Sunset place and mail addressed to their numbers on Orange street is not delivered.
excerpts.note: ★ Official name and used name diverging, with the post office following the used name.

excerpts.text: This portion of Orange street is not a logical continuation of the Orange street running directly east and west, and it is probable the petition will be granted.
excerpts.note: Asked only — the outcome is not in this clip.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Sept. 30, 1910 — "Ordinance to Change Many Street Names": the annexation renaming rule, and what a street name change costs the city

excerpts.text: After months of hard work the engineering department is almost ready to present the ordinance changing the names of a number of the streets in the annexed districts. The changes are made necessary by the fact that street names in the annexed portions are the same in many cases as those in the original city. Before the ordinance is presented to the council it will be submitted to the board of public works, probably next Wednesday, which is called "engineer's" day by the board.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Ordinance to Change Many Street Names / Nomenclature of Many Highways in Annexed District Will Be Altered."

excerpts.text: In nearly all cases the names of the streets in the original city are to be left as they are and those in the annexed portions changed. This means that Beacon street in San Pedro, one of the principal streets in the harbor suburb, will lose its name and the Beacon street in Los Angeles will retain it. There is a First street in San Pedro, East and West First streets in Wilmington and First street in Los Angeles. As there is no possible way these streets can be joined to each other the harbor streets will be called something else.
excerpts.note: ★ THE ANNEXATION RULE. The original city keeps its names.

excerpts.text: All the numbered streets of Wilmington and San Pedro will have to be changed for they have their counterparts in the original city. Streets in Hollywood and Colegrove, where the names conflict, will also have to be called something else.

The city engineer does not expect to have the ordinance adopted without a struggle for he expects objection from those persons who have quietly lived on one street many years and have to accustom themselves to another street running past their doors.

J. J. Johnson, asisstant city engineer, said yesterday that every time the council ordered the name of a street changed it costs the engineering department about $100 to change the name on its records, maps, profiles and other documents that bear street names.
excerpts.note: ★ The cost of a renaming, ca. 1910: about $100 per street. "asisstant" is the Herald's typo.

excerpts.text: The council has ordered a number of such changes, some of them without apparently good reasons. Last Tuesday it instructed the engineer to change the name of Newman street to Duin street. The petition that asked for the change was signed by several property owners and give as a reason for the change that Duin was an old settler and his name should be commemorated.
excerpts.note: Newman street → Duin street, ordered Tuesday, Sept. 27, 1910. A commemorative naming, and the engineer's example of a bad reason.

excerpts.text: The engineering department has no special objection to encouraging sentiment except in cases where it costs $100 or more to do so as when street names are changed.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Feb. 8, 1911 — "Plan to Rename Wesley Ave. Goes to Committee": the council votes 6 to 3 for University avenue, then reconsiders and sends it to committee

excerpts.text: Because of the two extra council meetings held last week there was not much for the council to do yesterday, but when the city legislators get together they feel they have to earn their $100 a month so, to make up for the lack of work yesterday, they did several things over after they had once disposed of them.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Plan to Rename Wesley Ave. Goes to Committee / Councilman Williams Opposes the Paving of Hoover Street." "Yesterday" = Feb. 7, 1911. Councilmen were paid $100 a month.

excerpts.text: The first thing was the changing of the name of Wesley avenue, from Jefferson to Santa Monica, to University avenue. A petition asking for this change of name had been submitted by the University of Southern California and other property owners on the street. The city engineer reported against the proposed change on the ground that as the name Wesley avenue had been attached to the street for 30 years some confusion would arise by changing it.
excerpts.note: ★ QUALIFIED: Jefferson to Santa Monica. "Attached to the street for 30 years" dates the name Wesley avenue to about 1881.

excerpts.text: Councilman Williams, who lives in that district, insisted that the engineer's recommendation be set aside and that he be instructed to present an ordinance changing the name to University avenue. Williams' motion carried by a vote of 6 to 3, Gregory, O'Brien and Stewart voting against it. After it was declared carried O'Brien started a campaign that lasted 15 or 20 minutes and finally had the matter reconsidered and sent to the streets committee.
excerpts.note: ★ Carried 6 to 3, then reconsidered and committed — all in one meeting. A minute book showing only the vote would mislead.

excerpts.text: Then the council instructed the city engineer to prepare an ordinance to pave Hoover street, from Twenty-eighth to Thirty-second, leaving the portion between Thirty-second and Jefferson without a pavement. After this had carried O'Brien conducted another campaign for reconsideration and won again. The matter was sent to the streets committee and that committee is likely to insist that the portion of the street between Thirty-second and Jefferson be paved. If it is, Councilman Williams will be stung for about $15000 assessment as he owns property fronting on the street. He was vigorously opposed to the pavement.
excerpts.note: Hoover Street — cf. the 1895 Hoover Street standing rule in handbook/MINUTES-TO-CHECK.md.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Jan. 29, 1917 — "Fight Over Plan to Change Street Name": two factions in The Palms clash over Valley street to Hughes street

excerpts.text: Two factions in The Palms today clashed before the city council over the proposed change of name of Valley street, The Palms, to Hughes street. "Questionable methods" were charged.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Fight Over Plan to Change Street Name."

excerpts.text: Protest against any such change was made by J. V. Lehigh, who has a 1200-foot property on Valley street. He said Valley street had been so known for twenty-five years. He declared it was the connecting link between Washington and National boulevards.
excerpts.note: Dates the name Valley street back to about 1892.

excerpts.text: "This change," said Lehigh, "is an insult to the people of The Palms. Some time ago the people voted on an annexation question and annexation was defeated. Then they held a second annexation election and cut out 250 taxpayers from the election district by questionable methods. These taxpayers were known to be against annexation. They carried the second election. Now they want to change the name of Valley street to Hughes street as a further insult to us."

It was explained that Thomas Hughes, now a harbor commissioner, was one of the annexation faction leaders and the renaming of the street was after him. On motion of Councilman Wright the ordinance changing the name of Valley street was held up for further consideration.
excerpts.note: HELD UP. Not law.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Feb. 14, 1917 — the council orders the Chinatown alley renamed, declaring its name a slur

excerpts.text: The name of "nigger alley," in the Chinatown section, is to be changed after having borne that title half a century. The city council, declaring the name "nigger" a slur upon the colored people, ordered the city engineer to prepare an ordinance changing the name to something else.
excerpts.note: asWritten, per MODEL-SPEC §12. Headline: "To Change Name of Chinatown Street." DO NOT reuse this wording in any public note. No replacement name is chosen here.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Sept. 30, 1919 — Sawtelle annexation upheld; an ordinance drafted renaming Sawtelle streets after Civil War battles

excerpts.text: The state supreme court has placed the stamp of approval on the annexation of Sawtelle to Los Angeles in denying Charles Coe a hearing on his appeal from the decision of the district court of appeal, which held that the annexation election was valid.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Supreme Court O. K.s Sawtelle Annexation; Ordinance Is Drafted."

excerpts.text: The city council today perused an ordinance changing the names of many streets in this new part of Los Angeles. The existing names conflict with street names in the old city. The new street names in Sawtelle district will carry the veterans of the Civil War residing at the Soldiers' Home back to their fighting days.
excerpts.note: "Today" = Sept. 30, 1919.

excerpts.text: Names of famous battles—Shiloh, Antietam, Appomattox, Corinth, Petersburg, Chickamauga, Vicksburg, Booneville—and many others will be used; also the names of many of the states will figure in the ordinance.
excerpts.note: Examples, not the list. Eight of "many others."

title: Los Angeles Herald, Nov. 27, 1919, p. 42 — “No Changes at Present”: the council declines to rename streets in San Pedro, and orders Reservoir Street to become Descanso Drive and part of Boyleston Avenue and Sapphire Street to become Huntley Drive

excerpts.text: NO CHANGES AT PRESENT. For the present, at least, the city council will not order any changes of street names in San Pedro. The council ordered the name of Reservoir street, from Sunset boulevard to Micheltorena street, changed to Descanso drive, and the name of that part of Boyleston avenue and Sapphire street, from north of Third, changed to Huntley drive.
excerpts.note: The entire item, four sentences. The headline is about the first sentence only.

excerpts.text: the name of that part of Boyleston avenue and Sapphire street, from north of Third, changed to Huntley drive
excerpts.note: ★★ THE SOURCE `sapphire` WAS MISSING. Two streets folded into one new name, which is why Garrigues could describe the result as running “between Boylston and Bixel” — Boylston Avenue's northern end and Sapphire Street were the two pieces. ⚠ Note the paper's spelling, BOYLESTON with an E, against the corpus's `boylston`; the 1897 council amendments that coined the name spell it Boylston, so this is the Herald's slip, not a variant worth carrying. ⚠ Note also that this renaming ran the opposite way from the one in documents/lah-1897-12-07, where Sapphire is a landmark used to locate another street (“Jewel street, Sapphire street to north termination, changed to Bixel street”): in 1897 Sapphire is the fixed point, in 1919 it is the thing being renamed.

excerpts.text: The council ordered the name of Reservoir street, from Sunset boulevard to Micheltorena street, changed to Descanso drive
excerpts.note: ★ Descanso Drive's naming, and a Reservoir Street that is NOT the one in the Oct. 1888 committee list (that one was in the Park Tract and became Centennial — see documents/lah-1888-10-11 item 41). This is the Silver Lake reservoir, and the stretch named runs north of this project's OSM extract, so no row is entered. Neither name is an entity here yet.

excerpts.text: For the present, at least, the city council will not order any changes of street names in San Pedro.
excerpts.note: Context for the whole 1909–1930 harbor-consolidation problem: a second platted grid with its own duplicate names, annexed into a city that had spent 1888–97 eliminating exactly that. The council declines the job here.

title: Los Angeles Herald, Aug. 12, 1920 — ordinance adopted changing a section of Cleland avenue in Mount Washington to Cynthia avenue

excerpts.text: The city council today adopted an ordinance changing the name of a section of Cleland avenue in the Mount Washington district, to Cynthia avenue. The section of the thoroughfare in which the change of name is authorized is a short street running off Cleland avenue.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Change Street Name." "Today" = Aug. 12, 1920. Extent given by description, not cross streets.

title: Los Angeles Herald, June 8, 1926 — protests heard on renaming Sherman way to Van Nuys boulevard, on a 74 per cent property owners' petition against

excerpts.text: Protests against the proposed ordinance changing the name of Sherman way to Van Nuys boulevard, through the city of Van Nuys, were heard by the city council today, at a hearing on the 74 per cent property owners' petition against the change. The ordinance also proposed to change the name of eWst Sherman way to Sherman way.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Protests Heard on Renaming Street." "eWst" is the Herald's typo for "West". "Today" = June 8, 1926.

title: Los Angeles Herald, June 17, 1926 — ordinance passed changing Wooddale avenue in Hollywood to Hollywood way

excerpts.text: The city council has passed an ordinance changing the name of Wooddale avenue in Hollywood to Hollywood way.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Change Street Name."

title: Los Angeles Herald, June 29, 1927 — "Final Action Due on Main St. Change": the ordinance would make Main street into Huntington drive from Mission road to S street, Wilmington

excerpts.text: Main street may officially disappear from the maps of Los Angeles today. The city council was scheduled to give final consideration to a formal ordinance changing the name of the old thoroughfare to Huntington drive.
excerpts.note: Headline: "Final Action Due on Main St. Change / Name for Old Thoroughfare Before Council."

excerpts.text: Acting under instructions from the councilmen, who voted 10 to 4 yesterday to have the ordinance prepared, the city attorney was to present the document changing the street's name today, with the action expected to be placed immediately before Mayor George E. Cryer for signature unless one of the dissenting councilmen votes against suspension of the rules. Objection to such suspension would mean that the measure would have to go through the regular series of meetings.
excerpts.note: Vote of 10 to 4 on June 28, 1927 — see documents/lae-1927-06-29 for the names of the four.

excerpts.text: Final effort to block the name change were made yesterday before council, but these were unsuccessful. Intimations made that a referendum would be circulated among the voters if the ordinance is passed today, but advocates of the new name for the old street expressed belief that this request for a veto by the electorate would not meet with success.
excerpts.note: "Final effort … were made" as printed.

excerpts.text: Under the provisions of the ordinance Main street will become Huntington drive from the northeast city limits at Mission road to S street in the Wilmington district.
excerpts.note: ★ The full proposed extent: Mission road to S street, Wilmington. The ordinance was never enacted.

title: Los Angeles Council minutes, Feb. 3, 1890 — petition No. 126 of Fred L. Alles et al. to change the name of Fort Street to Broadway (ledger p. 240)

excerpts.text: 126. From Fred L. Alles et al, asking that the name of Fort street be changed to Broadway. Referred to the Board of Public Works.

title: Los Angeles Council minutes, Apr. 10, 1893 — regular meeting (ledger pp. 527-560), including petition No. 465 of Fred L. Alles et al. to open Broadway north to Buena Vista Street

excerpts.text: No. 465. From Fred L. Alles et al. asking Council to appropriate the sum of $25,000. to assist in the Opening of Broadway North to Buena Vista street. Which was referred to the Board of Public Works.
excerpts.note: Ledger p. 555. The Alles of documents/min-1890-02-03, three years on. Where it leads: the Board of Public Works' report back, in the weeks after Apr. 10.

excerpts.text: The minutes of the last meeting of April 3rd. 1893 were read and approved.
excerpts.note: Ledger p. 527. The meeting that adopted Ordinance No. 1613 (documents/ord-1613) and whose own minutes are missing from the City Clerk's holdings — this line is the proof it took place.

excerpts.text: On motion of Mr. Pessell the Street Superintendent was ordered by the following vote, to open 16th street between Maple avenue and San Pedro street. Ayes Messrs. Campbell, Innes, Munson, Nickell, Pessell, Rhodes and Strohm, 7. Nays none.
excerpts.note: Ledger p. 545, and three weeks after the Miguel Subdivision (documents/mr053-016, Mar. 25, 1893) letters “16th ST. (formerly Pine St)” one block west. NO ROW: an order to OPEN a street is a claim about pavement being made, not about a name already lettered on ground, and the model has no kind for it. Left here until that is settled.

excerpts.text: No. 473. From Poindexter and List asking permission to lay a cement sidewalk in front of their property on Alpine street between Centennial avenue and Upper Main street by private contract. Which was referred to the Board of Public Works.
excerpts.note: Ledger p. 556. Six years after Virgin Street became Alpine (documents/ord-1887-08-22), and east of the Yale-to-Beaudry stretch that ordinance's grading resolution describes. NO ROW: “Upper Main street” may be historic Main or the modern street, and “Centennial avenue” is a generic away from the modern Centennial Street it probably is — neither end is safe to resolve from this sentence alone (Kenny, 2026-09-06).

excerpts.text: 7th. Final Ordinance establishing the grade of Ocean View Avenue from Alvarado Street to Bonnie Brae Street. Which Ordinance was referred to the Councilman from the Third Ward.
excerpts.note: Ledger p. 553. Ocean View Avenue is the corridor that became Beverly Boulevard — which is also what the 1884 Glassell plat's Diamond Street became through its own tract. Two names on one modern corridor, and where one stopped and the other started is the question the `diamond-street` identity decision turns on.

excerpts.text: Mr. Innes moved that the Street Superintendent be instructed to place a wooden culvert at the intersection of Fremont avenue and Diamond Street. Which was referred to the Board of Public Works.
excerpts.note: Ledger p. 539. Modern Diamond Street and Fremont Avenue meet at 0 m (34.05890, -118.25260), so this is the SURVIVING Diamond Street rather than the Glassell tract's stretch — the first evidence outside the 1884 plat that the name was in live use, though it settles the merge neither way.

excerpts.text: 5th. Ordinance of intention to grade Fifteenth Street from the Westerly line of Grand Avenue to the Easterly line of Hope street under Specifications No. 9 and to construct a cement curb on said Street between said points as per petition No. 460 from A. J. Bradish.
excerpts.note: Ledger p. 552. A west-side block of a street whose only other sighting is on the far side of downtown. The specification number is an uncertain reading.

excerpts.text: The matter of the hearing of the protest of W. Cole Trustee, et al. No. 434 against the contemplated opening of Twenty first street from Bonsallo avenue to Balboa street coming on regularly as a special order at this hour the same was taken up and the City Engineer reported that said protest does not represent a majority of the frontage of property within the district of assessment for opening said street. On motion of Mr. Teed the said protest was sustained and all proceedings abandoned.
excerpts.note: Ledger p. 545. Two things worth keeping: a street opening that did NOT happen — a shape the model has no row for — and “Balboa street”, a name that is in no sheet of this corpus and outside the OSM extract. Note also that the protest was sustained although the City Engineer had just reported it did not represent a majority.

title: Los Angeles Council minutes, Aug. 31, 1896 — adoption of Ordinance No. 3829 (New Series), “changing the names of certain streets in the City of Los Angeles” (ledger p. 205; recorded Ordinance Book 11 p. 460)

excerpts.text: 12th. Ordinance changing the names of certain streets in the City of Los Angeles. Draft of an ordinance of the Mayor and Council of the City of Los Angeles changing the names of certain streets in said city was read. On motion of Mr. Teed the rules were suspended and on motion of the same gentleman said ordinance was then adopted by the Council by the following vote: Ayes- Messrs. Ashman, Blanchard, Kingery, Munson, Pessell, Snyder, Stockwell and Pres. Teed 8. Noes- none. (Said ordinance will be found recorded in book 11 at page 460 of ordinances.)
excerpts.note: The margin beside this item is stamped “ORDINANCE No. 3829 NEW SERIES”. The prose never names a street: what the ordinance changed has to come from documents/lah-1896-09-03 until Book 11 p. 460 is in hand.

title: Los Angeles Council minutes, Sept. 8, 1896 — Ordinance No. 3847 (New Series), changing the names of nine streets in the southwest portion of the city (ledger p. 252; recorded Ordinance Book 11 p. 496)

excerpts.text: 2nd. Ordinance changing the names of certain streets in the southwest portion of the city as follows: Freeman Street to Twentieth Street. Olivia Street to Twenty-first Street. Bryant Avenue to Twenty-second Street. Cypress Avenue to Twenty-second Street. Maxwell Avenue to Twenty-third Street. Forrester Avenue to Twenty-fourth Street. Vine Street to Twenty-fourth Street. Clinton Avenue to Twenty-fifth Street. Kenwood Avenue to Twenty-fifth Street.
excerpts.note: The instrument as the clerk copied it — nine changes, six numbers, and no extents, which the ordinance itself had (documents/lah-1896-09-09). Two words here are the manuscript's weakest: “Vine”, faint enough that an earlier pass read it as “Pine”, and “Forrester”, which the Herald prints with two r's. Both are settled by the printed text, not by the hand.

excerpts.text: Draft of an ordinance of the Mayor and Council of the City of Los Angeles changing the names of certain streets in said city, was read. On motion of Mr. Teed the rules were suspended and on motion of the same gentleman said ordinance was then adopted by the Council by the following vote: Ayes Messrs. Ashman, Blanchard, Kingery, Munson, Pessell, Savage, Snyder, Stockwell and Pres. Teed (9). (Said ordinance will be found recorded in book 11 at page 496 of ordinances.)
excerpts.note: The margin beside the item is stamped “ORDINANCE No 3847 NEW SERIES”; the last digit is the least certain part of the reading and could be a 2. Same book as Ord. 3829 of Aug. 31 (p. 460), thirty-six pages later, and the same mover — Teed suspends the rules for both. Savage has joined the council since Aug. 31; the vote is 9 rather than 8.

title: Los Angeles Council minutes, Sept. 14, 1896 — petitions No. 816 and No. 817, asking that street names south and southwest of the city be brought into line with those north of Pico Street (ledger p. 295)

excerpts.text: No. 816- From Geo Harlan et al, asking that the names of certain streets in the South Side Tract be changed so as to make them compare with the names of the streets on the north side of Pico Street. Referred to the City Engineer.
excerpts.note: The motive, stated by the people asking for it. Worth more than most of the ordinances: it says what the campaign was FOR.

excerpts.text: No. 817- From C. O. Morgan et al, asking that certain streets in that portion of Los Angeles County lying adjacent to the City of Los Angeles on the southwest be changed as set forth in said petition. Referred to the City Engineer.
excerpts.note: The same ground the Sept. 8 ordinance had just renamed, but OUTSIDE the city — county territory adjacent to it. Renaming there was not the council's to do, which may be why this one goes to the City Engineer and vanishes. Note the petitioner's surname: a C. O. Morgan, where the 1882 Orchard Tract was G. W. Morgan's (documents/mr005-005). No connection established.

excerpts.text: No. 818- From John A. Bullard, asking that the limits of Fire District No 4 be changed to make the northerly line of said district the center line of Wilmington Street between First and Requena Streets. Referred to the Board of Fire Commissioners.
excerpts.note: Kept only for the two names: Wilmington Street and REQUENA Street, both of them downtown streets this project does not yet have. Requena is a lost street and this dates it alive in Sept. 1896.

excerpts.text: No. 821- From J. C. Kays et al, asking the Council to accept the proposition submitted to the Park Commissioners by Mr. E. F. Kysor for the establishment of a park in the Central Park Tract on Central Avenue, bounded north by Kysor Street, east by Central Avenue, south by Perry Street and west by Park Avenue…
excerpts.note: Kept for the boundary, which is four street names at once on ground next to Central Avenue — and for Kysor Street, named for the man making the offer, which is the tract-owner pattern happening in real time.

title: Los Angeles Council minutes, Sept. 21, 1896 — petition No. 829 to move the name Albion Street onto Stearns Avenue and rename the old Albion Street West Albion Street (ledger p. 334)

excerpts.text: No. 829- From S. Regelein et al, asking that the name of Stearns Avenue be changed to Albion Street, and Albion Street from Stearns Avenue to east Main Street be changed to West Albion Street. Referred to the Board of Public Works.
excerpts.note: A name moving sideways between two streets, with the loser keeping a modified form of it. Note that only the second half carries an extent. “Regelein” is an uncertain reading.

excerpts.text: No. 828- From J. C. Kolf et al, asking that Towne Avenue between Eighth and Twelfth Streets, be graded, graveled, curbed, sidewalked with cement five feet wide and sewered. Referred to the Board of Public Works.
excerpts.note: Kept as a dated attestation of Towne Avenue between Eighth and Twelfth — the entity is `towne-ave`, named in the Southern Pacific run on the Wolfskill orchard. No row: the request is about paving, not about the name, and the extent it gives is the work's, not the street's.

excerpts.text: No. 831- From S. C. Garner, stating that in the fall of 1894 he worked as a laborer on the grading of Second Street from Soto Street to Mott Street for T. A. Grant, Street Contractor, for which labor he has not been paid…
excerpts.note: Kept for Mott Street, which is the Mott of the 1869 Mott Tract (documents/mr001-489) alive as a street name a generation later, and for the fact that Second Street was being graded that far east in 1894. “Soto” is an uncertain reading.

excerpts.text: No. 827- From H. G. Wilshire et al, asking that Sixth Street west of Carondelet Street be graded and graveled. Referred to the Board of Public Works.
excerpts.note: H. Gaylord Wilshire, thirteen years before the boulevard carried his name, petitioning about the street west of Carondelet. Kept because the man is a street name in waiting, not because the item says anything about one.

title: Harris Newmark, Sixty Years in Southern California, 1853–1913, Containing the Reminiscences of Harris Newmark (2nd ed., New York: Knickerbocker Press, 1916)

excerpts.text: Temple Street had not then been opened by Beaudry and Potts, although there was a little cul-de-sac extending west from Spring Street; and at the junction of what is now Spring and Temple streets, there was a two-story adobe building in which D. W. Alexander and Francis Mellus conducted a general merchandise business.
excerpts.note: ★★ p. 61. The clause that cracked `potts-st`. Newmark is describing the town as he found it in 1853, so “had not THEN been opened” dates the Beaudry–Potts partnership to after that and before Temple Street existed — comfortably before the 1875 sheet that letters Potts Street on Beaudry's own subdivision. The earlier rejection of J. W. Potts turned on his joining the Common Council only in Dec. 1877; this shows the Council was never the relevant date.

excerpts.text: J. Wesley Potts was an early arrival, having tramped across the Plains all the way from Texas, in 1852, reaching Los Angeles in September. At first, he could obtain nothing to do but haul dirt in a hand-cart for the spasmodic patching-up of the streets; but when he had earned five or six dollars in that way, he took to peddling fruit, first carrying it around in a basket. Then he had a fruit stand. Getting the gold-fever, however, Potts went to the mines; but despairing at last of realizing anything there, he returned to Los Angeles and raised vegetables, introducing, among other things, the first locally-grown sweet potatoes put on the market. Later he was widely known as a “weather prophet” — with predictions quite as likely to be worthless as to come true.
excerpts.note: ★ p. 126. Newmark's own index runs the two passages together — “Potts, J. Wesley, 61, 126” — which is what identifies the Temple Street partner with this man, rather than leaving two Pottses in play. ⚠ Note the man Newmark draws: a street-patcher turned fruit peddler turned market gardener. Nothing here says landowner or subdivider; the standing that would put his name on a street comes from the partnership with Beaudry, not from this biography.

title: Ordinance No. 1613 (New Series), “An Ordinance changing the names of Wyoming avenue and Cooper street, in the city of Los Angeles” — adopted Apr. 3, 1893, approved Apr. 6, published in the Los Angeles Herald Apr. 9, 1893

excerpts.text: AN ORDINANCE CHANGING THE NAMES of Wyoming avenue and Cooper street, in the city of Los Angeles.

SECTION 1. That the names of Wyoming avenue and Cooper street, in the city of Los Angeles, are hereby abolished, and that said streets shall hereafter be known as one street, the name of which shall be Scott avenue.
excerpts.note: Two streets abolished and replaced by one. No extent is stated for either, which makes both changes unqualified (amendment §2).

excerpts.text: SEC. 2. The city clerk shall certify to the passage of this ordinance and shall cause the same to be published once in the Los Angeles Daily HERALD, and thereupon and thereafter the same shall take effect and be in force.
excerpts.note: The publication requirement, and the reason this ordinance survives at all: the minutes for Apr. 3, 1893 are missing, but the law made printing it a condition of its taking effect. handbook/RENAMING-SOURCES.md §2b.

excerpts.text: I hereby certify that the above ordinance was adopted by the council of the City of Los Angeles, at its meeting of the 3d day of April 1893. C. A. LUCKENBACH, City Clerk. Approved by me this 6th day of April, 1893. T. E. ROWAN, Mayor of the city of Los Angeles.
excerpts.note: Luckenbach is the same City Clerk who signs the Apr. 10, 1893 minutes (documents/min-1893-04-10).

rows.note: Half of a merger: this ordinance abolishes two names at once and puts one in their place. Nothing in the corpus letters Wyoming Avenue, so the row records the act and lands on no ground.
The other half. Same instrument, same day, same new name.

title: “An Ordinance Changing the names of Certain Streets in the City of Los Angeles” — Los Angeles Common Council, adopted Feb. 26, 1874 (council minutes, ledger p. 621)

excerpts.text: The following Ordinance was presented and read, and the same was adopted by the following vote — Aye Messrs. Dockweiler, Gerkens, Workman, Chaves, Mascarel and Sabichi
excerpts.note: The councillors' surnames are the least certain reading on the page; Sabichi and Dockweiler are corroborated by other 1870s-80s records in this project (J. H. Dockweiler surveyed the Wolfskill Orchard Tract in 1887).

excerpts.text: An Ordinance Changing the names of Certain Streets in the City of Los Angeles
The Mayor and Common Council of the City of Los Angeles do Ordain as follows

Sec 1. That the names of the three Streets in said City known and designated respectively as Grasshopper Street, Bull Street and Wasp Street be Changed as follows: Grasshopper Street to be named Pearl Street, Bull Street to be Castelar Street and Wasp Street to be Yale Street, and that henceforth the said Streets be respectively known and designated by the said names of Pearl Street, Castelar Street and Yale Streets.
Sec 2. This Ordinance shall take effect and be in force from and after its passage approval and publication.

rows.note: The Herald reported this one the next morning and not the other two.
The ordinance calls the old name “Wasp Street”; names.js records the entity as Hornet / Calle de las Avispas. Same lineage, third form of the ink — see the header.

title: “An Ordinance changing the name of Virgin Street” — Los Angeles Council, adopted Aug. 22, 1887 (council minutes, ledger pp. 700-701; ordinance number left blank in the ledger)

excerpts.text: The said ordinance was then on motion of Mr. Lovell adopted by Council by the following vote: Ayes, Councilmen, Collins, Frankenfield, Sibbs, Heyans, Kuhrts, Lovell, Teed, and President Breed (8); Noes, none.
excerpts.note: Frankenfield and Kuhrts are corroborated as Los Angeles councilmen of this period; “Sibbs”, “Heyans” and “Teed” are uncertain readings and want a second pass. None of them bears on the renaming.

excerpts.text: Ordinance No. — An Ordinance changing the name of Virgin Street. The Mayor and Council of the city of Los Angeles do ordain as follows: Section 1. That the name of that certain street in the City of Los Angeles known as Virgin shall be and is hereby declared to be changed to Alpine Street. Section 2. The Clerk of the Council shall certify to the passage of this ordinance and shall cause the same to be published once in the Los Angeles Daily Tribune and thereupon and thereafter it shall take effect and be in force.
excerpts.note: The ledger heading reads “Ordinance No.” with the number left blank.

excerpts.text: …the assessment to be levied for the collection of the amount necessary to pay the cost and expense of improving and grading said street shall be made upon property on both sides of said Virgin street, from its intersection with Yale street to the intersection with Beaudry street…
excerpts.note: Sec. 3 of a separate grading resolution earlier in the same session (ledger p. 700). Not part of the renaming; quoted because it is the only statement of where Virgin Street ran.

rows.name: virgin
rows.note: The resolution says the street runs at least from Yale to Beaudry; it does not say Virgin ran ONLY there, so this row claims that stretch and no more. “Beaudry street” is modern Beaudry Avenue — generic drift.
